docs.title: lexsync (Python)
docs.text:
Lexical optimisation and hardware-timed experiment generation.

lexsync builds psycholinguistic stimulus sets and the experiments that present them. Give it a word-frequency corpus in any of dozens of languages and a short design file, and it selects items matched in parallel across several lexical dimensions, counterbalances them across conditions and lists, and writes the experiment that runs them on PsychoPy, OpenSesame or in the browser through jsPsych, with EEG triggers bound to the flip on which the stimulus appears. A trial is described declaratively, so factorial word studies, lexical decision with generated pseudowords, priming, self-paced reading and cued categorisation all come out of the same engine and the same configuration file, as do the practice and filler blocks that run but are not analysed.

This is the feature-parity twin of the R package of the same name, which offers the same workflow in R. The two are documented separately but built from one repository and released under one version.

Get started API reference

docs.title: The two engines produce the same experiment
docs.text:
The R and Python engines produce byte-identical output: the same stimuli, and the same generated experiment down to the trial order. Nothing in the package draws a random number, so neither the platform's locale nor the last bit of a floating-point sum can change what comes out. A laboratory can run the R package and a collaborator the Python one, and the materials will agree rather than merely resemble each other. Continuous integration checks this on 22 worked designs across English, Spanish and Mandarin Chinese.

Two matching methods are a documented exception: mahalanobis and optimal rely on a covariance-matrix inverse and an assignment solver whose last bits differ between the two linear-algebra backends, so there the engines select equivalent sets, with byte identity no longer guaranteed. Each run's materials datasheet records which case applies. Reproducibility and parity sets out what the guarantee promises, how it is enforced and where it stops.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install lexsync

The corpora extra adds the wordfreq connector, which derives a lexicon for a language that is not bundled. The experiment extra adds PsychoPy and pyserial, and it is needed only to run a generated experiment on hardware. Generating one needs neither of them, only the core dependencies. An extra goes in brackets after the package name:

pip install "lexsync[corpora]"
pip install "lexsync[corpora,experiment]"

The development version comes straight from the repository, where the Python package sits in the python_workflow/ subdirectory:

pip install "git+https://github.com/pablobernabeu/lexsync.git#subdirectory=python_workflow"

See Getting started for what each extra carries, including the interpreters PsychoPy supports, and for the clone-based install that the 22 worked designs expect.

docs.title: Sixty seconds
docs.text:
The package bundles a 3000-word slice of an English lexicon and a copy of the global schema, so the example below runs immediately after installation, with no corpus to download and nothing to configure. It contrasts high- with low-frequency words while equating them, item by item, on length, orthographic neighbourhood density and OLD20.

from importlib.resources import files

import yaml

import lexsync

data = files("lexsync") / "data"
schema = yaml.safe_load((data / "schema.yaml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

design = {
    "name": "sixty_seconds",
    "language": "english",
    "n_per_condition": 60,
    "pool_filters": {"length": [3, 8], "frequency": [3.8, 7.0]},
    "conditions": [
        {"name": "high_frequency", "define_by": {"frequency": [5.2, 7.0]}},
        {"name": "low_frequency", "define_by": {"frequency": [3.8, 4.4]}},
    ],
    "match_on": ["length", "n_density", "old20"],
    "counterbalance": {"lists": 1},
}

lexicon = lexsync.load_lexicon(
    str(data / "en_example.csv"), schema, language="english"
)
pool = lexsync.build_pool(lexicon, design["pool_filters"])
stimuli = lexsync.match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)

report = lexsync.match_report(
    stimuli, ["length", "frequency", "n_density", "old20"], schema
)
print(report["comparisons"].to_string(index=False))

    condition      reference dimension  cohens_d  d_ci_low  d_ci_high  var_ratio  tost_p  equivalent  mean_diff role
low_frequency high_frequency    length     0.013    -0.290      0.316      0.944  0.0044        True      0.017 None
low_frequency high_frequency frequency     4.840     4.240      5.440      0.164  1.0000       False      1.545 None
low_frequency high_frequency n_density     0.062    -0.240      0.365      0.734  0.0091        True      0.367 None
low_frequency high_frequency     old20     0.005    -0.297      0.308      0.963  0.0039        True      0.002 None

The report is the point of the exercise, because it measures what the matching achieved. Frequency, the manipulation, separates the conditions by nearly five standard deviations. Each control dimension passes a two one-sided tests procedure against a bound of d = 0.5, so it is shown to be equivalent rather than merely failing to differ significantly. Matching and designs reads the report column by column.

Adding the experiment is two more calls. counterbalance assigns lists and a seeded trial order, and export_experiments writes all three targets from the same event list, listing every file it writes under files:

# illustrative: writes the generated experiment files into the working directory
import os

stimuli = lexsync.counterbalance(stimuli, design, schema)
paths = lexsync.export_experiments(
    stimuli, design, schema, outdir="output/experiments"
)
print(sorted(os.path.basename(p) for p in paths["files"]))

['sixty_seconds_english.html', 'sixty_seconds_english.osexp', 'sixty_seconds_english_opensesame.csv', 'sixty_seconds_english_opensesame_text.csv', 'sixty_seconds_english_psychopy.csv', 'sixty_seconds_english_psychopy.py']

The jsPsych file is self-contained apart from the library itself, so opening it in a browser runs the experiment. Every worked design in the repository is published that way, and the Demo link in the header opens the generated lexical-decision task. All 22 are listed at the demos index, including cued categorisation, a lexical decision carrying practice and filler blocks, relational priming over pairs, and a Mandarin Chinese contrast on a logographic script. A design with several counterbalancing versions has a link for each.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
Getting started covers installation, the command-line interface and the anatomy of a design file, which is where most of the work is done. From there the first three guides follow the arc of a study, and the fourth covers the same ground without any code.

  • Matching and designs: the pool, whether drawn from a lexicon or supplied as a list of your own, the four matching methods, the continuous alternative to dichotomising a predictor, resampling items as a random factor, and pseudoword generation.
  • Experiments and triggers: the declarative trial model, the six paradigms, counterbalancing, practice and filler blocks, and the three presentation targets, including where the EEG trigger is written and why that placement matters.
  • Reproducibility and parity: what the byte-identical guarantee promises, how it is enforced, and the materials datasheet that carries a set's provenance.
  • The app: the Streamlit front-end in the repository, which assembles a design through a browser tab, runs this same pipeline and exports the configuration and the code that reproduces the run.

Every public name is documented in the API reference, grouped as the R package's reference index is, and the works cited throughout are listed under References.

If lexsync contributes to published work, please cite it. Its citation gives the concept DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22906962, which resolves to the latest release archived on Zenodo.

docs.title: About
docs.text: lexsync is a cross-platform toolkit for psycholinguistics. It selects stimuli matched or controlled across several lexical dimensions, counterbalances them, and generates the experiment that presents them, with EEG triggers bound to stimulus onset on the laboratory targets. It ships as two structurally identical packages, one for R and one for Python, and the two select byte-identical stimuli under the deterministic matching methods.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
The tools in this area are capable but fragmented. Stimulus-control packages such as LexOPS, LIBRA and LASTU match words but stop before the experiment exists. Experiment builders such as PsychoPy and OpenSesame present stimuli but do not match them. The R and Python ecosystems rarely meet, and most matching tools target a single language. lexsync spans the whole path, from a many-language corpus through parallel multidimensional matching and counterbalancing to flip-locked experiment scripts, identically in both languages.

Beyond matching, it treats the stimulus set as a research artefact rather than a by-product. Each run emits a materials datasheet carrying its provenance, its checksums, the realised control with an effect size, a confidence interval and an equivalence test, and a pre-registration skeleton. A design is therefore something a reader can rerun.

docs.title: How to cite
docs.text:
Cite the software. The authoritative record is CITATION.cff at the root of the repository, which GitHub also renders into several formats through the 'Cite this repository' button. The reference for the current version of the Python package is:

Bernabeu, P. (2026). lexsync: Lexical optimisation and hardware-timed experiment generation. Python package version 0.1.1. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22906962

@Manual{lexsync,
  title  = {{lexsync}: Lexical optimisation and hardware-timed experiment generation},
  author = {Pablo Bernabeu},
  year   = {2026},
  note   = {Python package version 0.1.1},
  doi    = {10.5281/zenodo.22906962},
  url    = {https://pypi.org/project/lexsync/},
}

Copy BibTeX Download .bib

A manuscript describing lexsync is in preparation, under the title lexsync: A cross-platform pipeline for multidimensional lexical optimisation and hardware-timed experiment generation. It is unpublished and has no venue as yet. Once it is accepted, CITATION.cff will name it as the preferred citation, and until then the software reference above is the one to use. It gives the Zenodo concept DOI, which archives every release of the repository and so covers the Python package, since PyPI assigns no DOI. The R package's reference gives the DOI that CRAN assigned to it, https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.lexsync, which resolves to that package's page. CITATION.cff describes both packages, so it gives the Zenodo DOI and lists each package's identifiers.

Cite the corpus as well. The software citation covers the tool, not the data it drew your items from, and the corpora are third-party work with their own terms. Every one is cited, with its licence and retrieval date, in corpora/ATTRIBUTION.md, and each run's datasheet records which source file it read and its SHA-256.

docs.title: The developer
docs.text: lexsync is developed by Pablo Bernabeu, a researcher in the Department of Education at the University of Oxford, with hands-on experience of behavioural experiments, EEG, corpus analysis, computational modelling and statistics. He develops open, reproducible research software in R and Python, and is a Fellow of the Software Sustainability Institute. His ORCID record lists his other work.

docs.title: The two packages
docs.text:
This site documents the Python package, which is published on PyPI. The R package is documented at its own site and published on CRAN. The two are built from one repository and share one version number.

The R package Source on GitHub

Two browser front-ends also live in the repository, a Streamlit app over the Python engine and a Shiny app over the R engine. Each lets a researcher assemble a design without writing code and then exports the configuration and the one-line R, Python and command-line code that reproduces the run, so what the interface yields is a shareable artefact a reader can retrace. Both call their engine directly and need a local install, so neither is published beside this site. The app walks through the Streamlit one control by control, and apps/README.md covers launching either of them.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: The source code is under the MIT licence. The bundled corpus derivatives are under CC BY-SA 4.0 and are not covered by it. See Licence for the text and the distinction.

docs.title: Versioning and archival
docs.text: lexsync follows semantic versioning, and each release is tagged on GitHub, with the R and the Python package carrying the same version. The R package is on CRAN, which keeps the source of every version it publishes and gave the package the DOI mentioned above. The Python package is on PyPI. Zenodo archives every GitHub release, which carries both packages, and its concept DOI, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22906962, always resolves to the latest one. The reference above cites it and names the version, so it identifies the release as well. The changelog records what changed in each release.

docs.title: Contributing and support
docs.text: Bug reports and feature requests belong on the issue tracker. A report that includes the design YAML and the run log is one someone can act on, since between them they pin the inputs and every step that ran. The contributing guide describes the development setup for both engines and the parity rule that governs every change, and everyone taking part is asked to honour the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Every public name in lexsync is documented here, grouped along the path a study takes: reach a corpus, derive the dimensions, build a pool and match it, describe a trial, counterbalance it, report what the matching achieved, generate the experiment, and write down the provenance. The groups are the same ones the R package's reference index uses, so a name can be found in the same place on either site.

Everything listed under a group heading is importable straight from lexsync, with a handful of exceptions that are noted where they appear and are reached through their own module. Guides with worked examples are linked from the home page, and the published work that these entries cite is listed in full on the references page.

docs.title: Corpora and lexica
docs.text: Languages are supplied through a corpus registry, so reaching a new one takes a registry entry and no code. These functions find a corpus, download it into a per-user cache that can be cleared again, turn a corpus file in its publisher's layout into a lexicon, and read a derived lexicon or a prepared item table into the frame everything else expects.

docs.title: lexsync.list_corpora(registry_path=None)
lexsync.fetch_corpus(name, registry_path=None, n_words=10000, *, strict=False, exclude_latin=False)
docs.text:
Fetch a registered corpus into the cache.

name must be a single corpus name: one holding '/', '\' or ':' is refused before the registry is read, since the name becomes the cached file's name.

If name is a language code supported by the wordfreq connector, a lexicon is built with wordfreq from up to n_words of its most frequent forms that are spelt with letters. A form may hold combining marks, such as the vowel signs of Hindi and Bengali, and the zero-width non-joiner of Persian. It may also hold an apostrophe inside a Ukrainian word or a middle dot between two l's in a Catalan one, but no digit and no other punctuation mark. A lexicon left with fewer forms is reported on standard output, or refused with strict, and exclude_latin drops every form holding a Latin letter. These three arguments apply to the wordfreq connector only, and lexsync.corpora.build_wordfreq_lexicon gives the rule in full.

For any other name the registry entry's file is downloaded, once its URL's scheme has been checked. An entry's derived file, a lexicon already normalised, is fetched when it has one and cached as it arrives. Otherwise its openlexicon file is fetched and converted by :func:normalise_lexicon with the entry's columns and duplicates, so fetch_corpus("subtlex_us") caches a lexicon that :func:lexsync.load_lexicon reads. The transfer lands in a sidecar file that is renamed into the cache only after the size cap, the markup sniff, any registered sha256 and the normalisation have all passed. Every refusal names the registry file it read. A registry_path that does not exist is refused.

The file lands in :func:cache_dir. The cache directory is created only once the registry entry and its URL have been accepted, or the wordfreq lexicon built, so a refused call writes nothing. Each fetch into the cache begins by deleting any .part sidecar that an interrupted transfer left there more than a day earlier. The cache persists between sessions, and one corpus may reach the 200 MB download cap, so several of them add up. :func:cache_clear removes one corpus or the whole cache, and the next call fetches the corpus again.

Source code in src/lexsync/corpora.py 
def fetch_corpus(name: str, registry_path: str | None = None, n_words: int = 10000, *,
                 strict: bool = False, exclude_latin: bool = False) -> str:
    """Fetch a registered corpus into the cache.

    `name` must be a single corpus name: one holding '/', '\\' or ':' is refused
    before the registry is read, since the name becomes the cached file's name.

    If `name` is a language code supported by the wordfreq connector, a lexicon
    is built with wordfreq from up to `n_words` of its most frequent forms that
    are spelt with letters. A form may hold combining marks, such as the vowel
    signs of Hindi and Bengali, and the zero-width non-joiner of Persian. It may
    also hold an apostrophe inside a Ukrainian word or a middle dot between two
    l's in a Catalan one, but no digit and no other punctuation mark. A lexicon
    left with fewer forms is reported on standard output, or refused with
    `strict`, and `exclude_latin` drops every form holding a Latin letter. These
    three arguments apply to the wordfreq connector only, and
    ``lexsync.corpora.build_wordfreq_lexicon`` gives the rule in full.

    For any other name the registry entry's file is downloaded, once its URL's scheme
    has been checked. An entry's ``derived`` file, a lexicon already normalised, is
    fetched when it has one and cached as it arrives. Otherwise its ``openlexicon``
    file is fetched and converted by :func:`normalise_lexicon` with the entry's
    ``columns`` and ``duplicates``, so ``fetch_corpus("subtlex_us")`` caches a lexicon
    that :func:`lexsync.load_lexicon` reads. The transfer lands in a sidecar file that
    is renamed into the cache only after the size cap, the markup sniff, any registered
    sha256 and the normalisation have all passed. Every refusal names the registry
    file it read. A `registry_path` that does not exist is refused.

    The file lands in :func:`cache_dir`. The cache directory is created only once
    the registry entry and its URL have been accepted, or the wordfreq lexicon
    built, so a refused call writes nothing. Each fetch into the cache begins by
    deleting any ``.part`` sidecar that an interrupted transfer left there more
    than a day earlier. The cache persists between sessions, and one corpus may
    reach the 200 MB download cap, so several of them add up. :func:`cache_clear`
    removes one corpus or the whole cache, and the next call fetches the corpus
    again.
    """
    _check_corpus_name(name)
    reg_path, reg = _read_registry(registry_path)
    wf = reg.get("wordfreq_connector") or {}
    if name in (wf.get("languages") or []):
        df = build_wordfreq_lexicon(name, n_words, strict=strict, exclude_latin=exclude_latin)
        dest = os.path.join(_prepare_cache(), f"{name}_wordfreq.csv")
        # LF explicitly: pandas otherwise follows os.linesep, and the cached
        # lexicon's bytes (and any checksum of them) must not depend on the OS.
        df.to_csv(dest, index=False, encoding="utf-8", lineterminator="\n")
        print(f"lexsync: built '{name}' via wordfreq. Please cite: {wf.get('citation', '')}")
        return dest
    entry = (reg.get("corpora") or {}).get(name)
    if not entry:
        raise ValueError(f"lexsync: corpus '{name}' is not in the registry '{reg_path}'.")
    url, expected, normalise = _download_source(name, entry, reg_path)
    # A registry is editable, and fetch_corpus() writes wherever it points, so a
    # 'file://' or 'ftp://' entry would read a local path under the guise of a
    # download. Only the two schemes a corpus is published over are honoured.
    if not re.match(r"https?://", url, re.IGNORECASE):
        raise ValueError(
            f"lexsync: corpus '{name}' registers a non-http(s) URL ({url}) in "
            f"'{reg_path}'; refusing to download."
        )
    import urllib.error
    import urllib.request
    # Only now, with every refusal behind it, does the call touch the disk.
    dest = os.path.join(_prepare_cache(), f"{name}.csv")
    # The transfer lands in a sidecar and is renamed over `dest` only after every
    # check below has passed, so a truncated or unverified body can never sit at
    # the cache path, where a later run would trust it.
    part = dest + ".part"
    try:
        # 60 s guards against a stalled server, which urlretrieve() would wait on
        # forever; the R engine's download.file() honours options(timeout).
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=60) as response, \
                open(part, "wb") as handle:
            received = 0
            for chunk in iter(lambda: response.read(65536), b""):
                received += len(chunk)
                if received > _max_download_bytes():
                    raise ValueError(
                        "lexsync: corpus download exceeded the 200 MB size limit. "
                        "Retrieve the delimited file manually and pass it to "
                        "load_lexicon()."
                    )
                handle.write(chunk)
    except (urllib.error.URLError, OSError) as exc:
        if os.path.exists(part):
            os.remove(part)
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"lexsync: could not download corpus '{name}' from {url} ({exc}). "
            f"Check the URL in '{reg_path}', or download the file manually, convert it "
            f"with normalise_lexicon() and pass the result to load_lexicon()."
        ) from exc
    except ValueError:
        if os.path.exists(part):
            os.remove(part)
        raise
    if _starts_with_markup(part):
        os.remove(part)
        raise ValueError(
            f"lexsync: corpus '{name}' returned an HTML page, not a delimited file "
            f"({url}); the registry URL may have rotted. Retrieve the delimited file "
            f"manually and pass it to load_lexicon()."
        )
    # 'sha256' is optional per registry entry; when present the download must
    # match it before it may enter the cache.
    if expected and sha256_file(part) != expected:
        os.remove(part)
        raise ValueError(
            f"lexsync: checksum mismatch for corpus '{name}'; the download does "
            f"not match the registry's sha256. Retry the download, or verify the "
            f"sha256 recorded in '{reg_path}'."
        )
    if normalise:
        # The corpus file is read into memory and its sidecar then holds the lexicon,
        # so a file that cannot be normalised leaves nothing behind either.
        try:
            # The file's name and extension, without any query or fragment.
            named = re.sub(r"[?#].*$", "", url)
            lexicon, message = _normalise(part, None, entry, _delimiter_for(named),
                                          os.path.basename(named))
        finally:
            os.remove(part)
        print(message)
        write_csv_utf8(lexicon, part)
    os.replace(part, dest)
    print(f"lexsync: downloaded '{name}'. Please cite: {entry.get('citation', '(see registry)')}")
    return dest

docs.title: lexsync.normalise_lexicon(path, columns=None, entry=None, delimiter=None, out=None)
docs.text:
Turn a corpus file in its publisher's layout into a lexicon load_lexicon reads.

Reads a tab- or comma-separated file. delimiter names the separator, "," or "\t". Left as None, it is taken from the extension (.tsv and .tab are tab, .csv is comma) and otherwise from the header line, which is tab-separated when it holds a tab. A tab-separated file is read with no quoting.

columns maps lexsync's column names to the file's, as a registry entry's columns does: word, one of freq_zipf and freq_permillion, and optionally pos. entry is a registry entry, or the name of one in the registry lexsync finds by default (see :func:list_corpora), and supplies the map when columns is None and the duplicates rule. Without a map the file's own word, freq_zipf or freq_permillion, and pos columns are read.

Words are trimmed, lower-cased and put in Unicode NFC, as load_lexicon keys them, and rows missing a word or a frequency are dropped. A form that then appears more than once is resolved by duplicates: first (the default) keeps the first row in file order, and sum adds its rows' frequencies per million, as Lexique needs, since it splits a homograph's frequency between its rows. Frequencies per million are converted with Zipf = log10(per million) + 3, rounded to three places by lexsync's shared rounder. A value of 0 or below has no Zipf value and is refused. Zipf values read as they are must lie between 0 and 9.

The lexicon has the columns word, freq_zipf, then freq_permillion when Zipf was derived from it, and pos when the file has one, in the UTF-8 byte order of word. With out it is also written there, comma-separated with LF line endings. A line on standard output gives the number of forms, and for derived Zipf values the number that lay within 1e-9 of a rounding boundary after scaling. That is the only step at which the two engines' log10 could round a value apart, and the count is expected to be 0. attrs["normalisation"] holds {"n_read", "n_forms", "n_merged", "duplicates", "zipf_derived", "near_boundary"}, and a run over the lexicon records the boundary count in its run log and datasheet.

Mirrors normalise_lexicon in R_workflow/R/corpora.R, which writes the same bytes.

Source code in src/lexsync/corpora.py 
def normalise_lexicon(path: str, columns=None, entry=None, delimiter=None,
                      out: str | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Turn a corpus file in its publisher's layout into a lexicon load_lexicon reads.

    Reads a tab- or comma-separated file. ``delimiter`` names the separator, "," or
    "\\t". Left as None, it is taken from the extension (.tsv and .tab are tab, .csv is
    comma) and otherwise from the header line, which is tab-separated when it holds a
    tab. A tab-separated file is read with no quoting.

    ``columns`` maps lexsync's column names to the file's, as a registry entry's
    ``columns`` does: ``word``, one of ``freq_zipf`` and ``freq_permillion``, and
    optionally ``pos``. ``entry`` is a registry entry, or the name of one in the
    registry lexsync finds by default (see :func:`list_corpora`), and supplies the map
    when ``columns`` is None and the ``duplicates`` rule. Without a map the file's own
    ``word``, ``freq_zipf`` or ``freq_permillion``, and ``pos`` columns are read.

    Words are trimmed, lower-cased and put in Unicode NFC, as load_lexicon keys them,
    and rows missing a word or a frequency are dropped. A form that then appears more
    than once is resolved by ``duplicates``: ``first`` (the default) keeps the first
    row in file order, and ``sum`` adds its rows' frequencies per million, as Lexique
    needs, since it splits a homograph's frequency between its rows. Frequencies per
    million are converted with Zipf = log10(per million) + 3, rounded to three places
    by lexsync's shared rounder. A value of 0 or below has no Zipf value and is
    refused. Zipf values read as they are must lie between 0 and 9.

    The lexicon has the columns ``word``, ``freq_zipf``, then ``freq_permillion`` when
    Zipf was derived from it, and ``pos`` when the file has one, in the UTF-8 byte
    order of ``word``. With ``out`` it is also written there, comma-separated with LF
    line endings. A line on standard output gives the number of forms, and for derived
    Zipf values the number that lay within 1e-9 of a rounding boundary after scaling.
    That is the only step at which the two engines' log10 could round a value apart,
    and the count is expected to be 0. ``attrs["normalisation"]`` holds ``{"n_read",
    "n_forms", "n_merged", "duplicates", "zipf_derived", "near_boundary"}``, and a run
    over the lexicon records the boundary count in its run log and datasheet.

    Mirrors normalise_lexicon in R_workflow/R/corpora.R, which writes the same bytes.
    """
    frame, message = _normalise(path, columns, entry, delimiter, os.path.basename(str(path)))
    print(message)
    if out is not None:
        write_csv_utf8(frame, out)
    return frame

docs.title: lexsync.corpora.build_wordfreq_lexicon(language, n_words=10000, min_len=2, max_len=15, *, strict=False, exclude_latin=False)
docs.text:
Build a (word, freq_zipf) lexicon for any wordfreq language.

Takes wordfreq's most frequent forms for language, lower-cased and in Unicode NFC, until n_words of them pass the letter filter and are min_len to max_len characters long. It looks no further than the first 3 * n_words forms. A form passes when it opens with a letter and every other character is a letter, a combining mark or a zero-width non-joiner or joiner. Hindi है and Bengali না, spelt with combining vowel signs, therefore pass, as do the many Persian forms spelt with a non-joiner. A Ukrainian or Belarusian form may also hold an apostrophe between two letters (п'ять), and a Catalan one a middle dot between two l's (pel·lícula). Digits never pass, and nor do underscores or any punctuation mark besides those joiners, so English contractions and French elisions stay out. Length counts code points, as the lexicon readers count it, so vowel signs, viramas and zero-width characters count. A form that wordfreq gives no frequency is dropped.

When the lexicon holds fewer than n_words forms, a line on standard output says so, and with strict the shortfall raises ValueError. exclude_latin drops every form holding a Latin letter, such as the English tokens in the Hindi list. It is not a one-script rule, so a Japanese lexicon keeps its kana and kanji together, and it leaves nothing of a language written in the Latin alphabet.

Raises ModuleNotFoundError if the optional [corpora] extra is not installed.

Source code in src/lexsync/corpora.py 
def build_wordfreq_lexicon(language: str, n_words: int = 10000,
                           min_len: int = 2, max_len: int = 15, *,
                           strict: bool = False,
                           exclude_latin: bool = False) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Build a (word, freq_zipf) lexicon for any wordfreq language.

    Takes wordfreq's most frequent forms for `language`, lower-cased and in Unicode
    NFC, until `n_words` of them pass the letter filter and are `min_len` to
    `max_len` characters long. It looks no further than the first 3 * `n_words`
    forms. A form passes when it opens with a letter and every other character is a
    letter, a combining mark or a zero-width non-joiner or joiner. Hindi है and
    Bengali না, spelt with combining vowel signs, therefore pass, as do the many
    Persian forms spelt with a non-joiner. A Ukrainian or Belarusian form may also
    hold an apostrophe between two letters (п'ять), and a Catalan one a middle dot
    between two l's (pel·lícula). Digits never pass, and nor do underscores or any
    punctuation mark besides those joiners, so English contractions and French
    elisions stay out. Length counts code points, as the lexicon readers count it,
    so vowel signs, viramas and zero-width characters count. A form that wordfreq
    gives no frequency is dropped.

    When the lexicon holds fewer than `n_words` forms, a line on standard output says
    so, and with `strict` the shortfall raises ValueError. `exclude_latin` drops every
    form holding a Latin letter, such as the English tokens in the Hindi list. It is
    not a one-script rule, so a Japanese lexicon keeps its kana and kanji together,
    and it leaves nothing of a language written in the Latin alphabet.

    Raises ModuleNotFoundError if the optional [corpora] extra is not installed.
    """
    # Deferred because wordfreq belongs to the [corpora] extra, so importing it at
    # module scope would break `import lexsync` on a default install. Guarded because
    # this is what `lexsync fetch fr` reaches, and the README advertises that command:
    # unguarded, a default install answers it with a bare ModuleNotFoundError nine
    # frames down, which names the missing module and no way to get it. Everything
    # else in this module answers a failure with the remedy, and so does this now.
    # The R twin has no counterpart here: Connector B is Python-only, and R/corpora.R
    # reads its pre-derived output as an ordinary lexicon.
    try:
        import wordfreq
    except ImportError as exc:
        raise ModuleNotFoundError(
            f"lexsync: building a lexicon for '{language}' needs the wordfreq connector, "
            f"which ships in the optional [corpora] extra and is not installed. Install "
            'it with: pip install "wordfreq>=3.0,<4".'
        ) from exc

    words: list[str] = []
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for token in wordfreq.top_n_list(language, n_words * 3):
        # NFC after lower-casing, the order in which load_lexicon normalises a word. A
        # form that wordfreq gives decomposed, as it gives some Greek ones, then keeps
        # its marks, is stored as the readers will key it and is kept only once.
        w = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", token.lower())
        if (w in seen or not min_len <= len(w) <= max_len
                or not _spelt_with_letters(w, language)
                or (exclude_latin and _has_latin_letter(w))):
            continue
        seen.add(w)
        words.append(w)
        if len(words) >= n_words:
            break
    zipf = [wordfreq.zipf_frequency(w, language) for w in words]
    df = pd.DataFrame({"word": words, "freq_zipf": np.round(zipf, 3),
                       "language": language, "source": "wordfreq"})
    df = df[df.freq_zipf > 0].sort_values("word").reset_index(drop=True)
    if len(df) < n_words:
        # A short lexicon thins every frequency band a design draws on, and a Hindi one
        # used to come back with 3,207 of the 10,000 forms asked for, and nothing said so.
        message = (f"lexsync: wordfreq supplied only {len(df)} forms for '{language}' "
                   f"that pass the letter filter (n_words was {n_words}).")
        if strict:
            raise ValueError(message)
        print(message)
    return df

Per-user cache directory for fetched corpora.

Where :func:fetch_corpus puts what it fetches, and the only place the package writes to without being handed a path. This function only reports the path. The directory is created by the first fetch into it, so until then it does not exist.

The cache persists between sessions. A registered corpus is a delimited word list, and a download is refused above 200 MB, so a cache holding several large corpora can reach a few hundred megabytes. Each fetch into the cache first deletes any partial download that an interrupted transfer left there more than a day earlier, and fetching a corpus again replaces the earlier copy. Fetched corpora otherwise stay until :func:cache_clear removes them, one corpus at a time or all together. Nothing kept there is irreplaceable, so the next call downloads afresh. The R twin documents the same contract in lexsync_cache_dir.Rd; only the location differs, since R uses tools::R_user_dir.

def cache_dir() -> str:
    """Per-user cache directory for fetched corpora.

    Where :func:`fetch_corpus` puts what it fetches, and the only place the
    package writes to without being handed a path. This function only reports
    the path. The directory is created by the first fetch into it, so until then
    it does not exist.

    The cache persists between sessions. A registered corpus is a delimited word
    list, and a download is refused above 200 MB, so a cache holding several
    large corpora can reach a few hundred megabytes. Each fetch into the cache
    first deletes any partial download that an interrupted transfer left there
    more than a day earlier, and fetching a corpus again replaces the earlier
    copy. Fetched corpora otherwise stay until :func:`cache_clear` removes them,
    one corpus at a time or all together. Nothing kept there is irreplaceable, so
    the next call downloads afresh. The R twin documents the same contract in
    lexsync_cache_dir.Rd; only the location differs, since R uses
    tools::R_user_dir.
    """
    return os.path.join(os.path.expanduser("~"), ".lexsync", "cache")

Remove fetched corpora from the cache.

Deletes what :func:fetch_corpus put in :func:cache_dir. Given a name, that is the corpus's <name>.csv, any <name>.csv.part that an interrupted download left behind and the <name>_wordfreq.csv lexicon the wordfreq connector builds. With name left as None it is the whole cache directory, and the ~/.lexsync directory above it once nothing else is left there. A corpus needed again is fetched afresh by the next :func:fetch_corpus call. Mirrors lexsync_cache_clear() in R_workflow/R/corpora.R, whose engine has no wordfreq connector and so no _wordfreq.csv to remove.

Returns the paths of the files removed, empty when there was nothing to remove. Raises OSError, naming them, when files survive the attempt (one held open on Windows, say).

Source code in src/lexsync/corpora.py 
def cache_clear(name: str | None = None) -> list[str]:
    """Remove fetched corpora from the cache.

    Deletes what :func:`fetch_corpus` put in :func:`cache_dir`. Given a `name`,
    that is the corpus's ``<name>.csv``, any ``<name>.csv.part`` that an
    interrupted download left behind and the ``<name>_wordfreq.csv`` lexicon the
    wordfreq connector builds. With `name` left as None it is the whole cache
    directory, and the ``~/.lexsync`` directory above it once nothing else is left
    there. A corpus needed again is fetched afresh by the next
    :func:`fetch_corpus` call. Mirrors lexsync_cache_clear() in
    R_workflow/R/corpora.R, whose engine has no wordfreq connector and so no
    ``_wordfreq.csv`` to remove.

    Returns the paths of the files removed, empty when there was nothing to
    remove. Raises OSError, naming them, when files survive the attempt (one held
    open on Windows, say).
    """
    cache = cache_dir()
    if name is None:
        if not os.path.isdir(cache):
            return []
        removed = sorted(os.path.join(root, fname)
                         for root, _dirs, files in os.walk(cache) for fname in files)
        targets = [cache]
        # Keep going past a file that cannot be deleted, as R's unlink() does, and
        # report what survives below.
        shutil.rmtree(cache, ignore_errors=True)
    else:
        _check_corpus_name(name)
        targets = [os.path.join(cache, f"{name}{suffix}")
                   for suffix in (".csv", ".csv.part", "_wordfreq.csv")]
        removed = [path for path in targets if os.path.isfile(path)]
        for path in removed:
            with contextlib.suppress(OSError):
                os.remove(path)
    left = [path for path in (targets if name is None else removed)
            if os.path.exists(path)]
    if left:
        raise OSError(f"lexsync: could not remove {', '.join(left)} from the cache; "
                      f"check that no other process is using it.")
    if name is None:
        # ~/.lexsync holds nothing but the cache, so an emptied one would be left
        # behind in the user's home. rmdir() removes it only when it is empty. R's
        # twin has no such step: the parent of its cache directory is shared by
        # every R package's cache.
        with contextlib.suppress(OSError):
            os.rmdir(os.path.dirname(cache))
    return removed

docs.text:
Load a derived lexicon and give it the inexpensive dimensions.

word is trimmed, lower-cased and normalised to Unicode NFC, and duplicates are then removed, keeping the first row in file order. When normalisation changed or merged any word, attrs["input_normalisation"] holds {"changed", "collapsed"}: the words it rewrote and the duplicate rows it removed.

A freq_zipf value outside 0 to 9 is refused: it is almost always a frequency per million in the wrong column (convert it with normalise_lexicon). A log count such as SUBTLEX-US's Lg10WF, log10(count + 1) and at most 6.33, passes the check and must still be converted, since it reads about 1.3 below Zipf. Mirrors load_lexicon in R_workflow/R/querying.R.

Source code in src/lexsync/querying.py 
def load_lexicon(path: str, schema: dict, language: str | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load a derived lexicon and give it the inexpensive dimensions.

    ``word`` is trimmed, lower-cased and normalised to Unicode NFC, and duplicates are
    then removed, keeping the first row in file order. When normalisation changed or
    merged any word, ``attrs["input_normalisation"]`` holds ``{"changed",
    "collapsed"}``: the words it rewrote and the duplicate rows it removed.

    A ``freq_zipf`` value outside 0 to 9 is refused: it is almost always a frequency per
    million in the wrong column (convert it with ``normalise_lexicon``). A log count such
    as SUBTLEX-US's ``Lg10WF``, log10(count + 1) and at most 6.33, passes the check and
    must still be converted, since it reads about 1.3 below Zipf. Mirrors load_lexicon
    in R_workflow/R/querying.R.
    """
    df = read_csv_utf8(path)
    validate_lexicon(df, schema)
    # `or {}` at every level: an empty `dimensions:` or `frequency:` key parses to
    # None here and to NULL in R, where `$` chains through it to the default. A
    # default argument only covers an ABSENT key, so the two engines answered the
    # same schema with a column name and an AttributeError.
    freq_col = ((schema.get("dimensions") or {}).get("frequency") or {}).get("column") or "freq_zipf"
    _require_numbers(df[freq_col], freq_col)
    # Filter before coercing: str() renders a missing word as the literal
    # string "nan", which survives both guards below, whereas the R engine (where
    # as.character(NA) stays NA) drops the row. Coercing first would therefore
    # desynchronise the two engines' row counts and shift every subsequent id.
    df = df[df["word"].notna() & df[freq_col].notna()].copy()
    df["word"] = _fold_words(df["word"])
    df = df[df["word"] != ""].copy()
    # The rows the lexicon keeps, before de-duplication, as the R engine checks them.
    zipf = df["freq_zipf"]
    if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(zipf) and not pd.api.types.is_bool_dtype(zipf):
        _check_zipf_range(zipf)
    # NFC before de-duplication, so the two spellings of a word are one word and the
    # first row in file order is the one kept.
    df["word"], changed, collapsed = _nfc_count(df["word"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="word")
    # An empty selection is never what the caller meant, and it fails far from
    # here: pandas would hand back a well-formed frame of nothing, while the R
    # engine dies on base R's "replacement has 1 row, data has 0". Both engines
    # raise this message instead, while the path is still in scope.
    if df.empty:
        raise ValueError(
            f"lexsync: lexicon '{path}' has no usable rows: it is empty, "
            f"or every row is missing 'word' or '{freq_col}'."
        )
    # Sort by UTF-8 byte order so the lexicon order is locale-independent and
    # identical to the R engine (which uses a 'radix' byte-order sort).
    df = (df.assign(_k=df["word"].map(lambda w: w.encode("utf-8")))
            .sort_values("_k").drop(columns="_k").reset_index(drop=True))
    df["id"] = np.arange(1, len(df) + 1)
    df["length"] = df["word"].str.len()
    df["n_syllables"] = _syllable_column(df["word"])
    df["frequency"] = df[freq_col].astype(float)
    if language is not None:
        df["language"] = language
    df = df.reset_index(drop=True)
    # Read by run_pipeline for the run log and the datasheet.
    record = _nfc_record(changed, collapsed)
    if record:
        df.attrs["input_normalisation"] = record
    return df

docs.text:
Load a paradigm item table (prime-target pairs, sentences, …).

The table must carry an item identifier, a condition label and the paradigm's presented fields. Field values are validated (no control characters; bounded length) so a crafted item cannot corrupt the generated loop table or scripts. Items are mapped to a deterministic integer set id (byte order) so counterbalancing matches the corpus path and the two engines. The item id, the condition and the presented fields are normalised to Unicode NFC. When that changed any cell, attrs["input_normalisation"] holds {"changed", "collapsed"}, with collapsed always 0 since no row is removed.

Source code in src/lexsync/querying.py 
def load_items(path: str, required_fields) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load a paradigm item table (prime-target pairs, sentences, …).

    The table must carry an ``item`` identifier, a ``condition`` label and the
    paradigm's presented fields. Field values are validated (no control
    characters; bounded length) so a crafted item cannot corrupt the generated
    loop table or scripts. Items are mapped to a deterministic integer ``set`` id
    (byte order) so counterbalancing matches the corpus path and the two engines.
    The item id, the condition and the presented fields are normalised to Unicode
    NFC. When that changed any cell, ``attrs["input_normalisation"]`` holds
    ``{"changed", "collapsed"}``, with ``collapsed`` always 0 since no row is removed.
    """
    parts = str(path).replace("\\", "/").split("/")
    if ".." in parts:
        raise ValueError("lexsync: items path must not contain '..'.")
    # The item id, the condition label and the paradigm's presented fields stay text.
    # Typed by their values, a column of response keys such as TRUE and FALSE would
    # become logical, and an `item` column of numbers would lose the zero of '01'. The
    # reader trims every cell and reads a blank, all-whitespace or 'NA' cell as
    # missing, in both engines (see read_csv_utf8).
    df = read_csv_utf8(path, as_character=["item", "condition"] + list(required_fields))
    needed = ["item", "condition"] + list(required_fields)
    missing = [c for c in needed if c not in df.columns]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"lexsync: items table '{path}' is missing column(s): {', '.join(missing)}.")
    # Missingness is tested before any string coercion: str() would render a missing
    # cell as the literal 'nan', which a blank condition then carries past the
    # hash-key guard downstream.
    for col in needed:
        if df[col].isna().any():
            raise ValueError(
                f"lexsync: the items table has missing value(s) in column '{col}'; "
                "every item, condition and presented field must be filled.")
    df = df.copy()
    # The item id, the condition and the presented text in NFC, as every other text
    # key is, so one item spelt two ways is one set and its text one string. A merged
    # spelling removes no row here, so only the changed cells are counted.
    changed = 0
    for col in dict.fromkeys(needed):
        df[col], n_changed, _ = _nfc_count(df[col].astype(str))
        changed += n_changed
    item_key = df["item"].astype(str)
    # A repeated item-condition pair is a slip that would silently duplicate a trial
    # in every generated list; the first repeat in file order is reported.
    seen = set()
    for it, cond in zip(item_key, df["condition"], strict=True):
        if (it, cond) in seen:
            raise ValueError(
                f"lexsync: the items table repeats item '{it}' for condition '{cond}'; "
                "each item and condition pair may appear once.")
        seen.add((it, cond))
    for f in [c for c in required_fields if c in df.columns]:
        df[f] = [clean_field(v, f) for v in df[f]]
    items = sorted(item_key.unique(), key=lambda s: s.encode("utf-8"))
    set_map = {it: i + 1 for i, it in enumerate(items)}
    df["set"] = item_key.map(set_map)
    df = df.reset_index(drop=True)
    record = _nfc_record(changed, 0)
    if record:
        df.attrs["input_normalisation"] = record
    return df

docs.title: lexsync.load_pool(path, schema, lexicon=None, language=None)
docs.text:
Load a supplied candidate pool of words and give it the matcher's dimensions.

A researcher who already has a curated word list (from a previous study, a norming session, a colleague) should not have to dress it up as a corpus lexicon to get lexsync's matching, validation and datasheet. This reads such a list and returns something the matcher accepts.

The list needs only a word column. Length and the syllable estimate are derived from the form. Everything else is either supplied on the list itself or looked up: with lexicon given, the corpus dimensions (frequency above all) are joined for those words, and a word the lexicon does not have is a hard error rather than a NaN, because the tolerance windows drop missing rows silently and the pool would then be smaller than the user believes it is.

The returned reference matters as much as the pool. n_density and old20 are properties of a word in its language, not among the handful of words a study happens to use, so computing them against a 200-word supplied list would give numbers that mean nothing. When a lexicon is given, the reference is the lexicon's words; only without one does it fall back to the pool itself. A reference_member column on whichever of the two supplies the reference keeps only the rows it marks 1.

Returns {"pool": DataFrame, "reference": list}. Words are trimmed, lower-cased and normalised to Unicode NFC as in load_lexicon, and the pool carries the same attrs["input_normalisation"] record when that changed or merged any word of the pool or the lexicon. Mirrors load_pool in R_workflow/R/querying.R.

Source code in src/lexsync/querying.py 
def load_pool(path: str, schema: dict, lexicon=None, language=None) -> dict:
    """Load a supplied candidate pool of words and give it the matcher's dimensions.

    A researcher who already has a curated word list (from a previous study, a norming
    session, a colleague) should not have to dress it up as a corpus lexicon
    to get lexsync's matching, validation and datasheet. This reads such a list and
    returns something the matcher accepts.

    The list needs only a ``word`` column. Length and the syllable estimate are derived
    from the form. Everything else is either supplied on the list itself or looked up:
    with ``lexicon`` given, the corpus dimensions (frequency above all) are joined for
    those words, and a word the lexicon does not have is a hard error rather than a
    NaN, because the tolerance windows drop missing rows silently and the pool would
    then be smaller than the user believes it is.

    The returned ``reference`` matters as much as the pool. ``n_density`` and ``old20``
    are properties of a word in its *language*, not among the handful of words a study
    happens to use, so computing them against a 200-word supplied list would give
    numbers that mean nothing. When a lexicon is given, the reference is the lexicon's
    words; only without one does it fall back to the pool itself. A
    ``reference_member`` column on whichever of the two supplies the reference keeps
    only the rows it marks 1.

    Returns ``{"pool": DataFrame, "reference": list}``. Words are trimmed, lower-cased
    and normalised to Unicode NFC as in ``load_lexicon``, and the pool carries the same
    ``attrs["input_normalisation"]`` record when that changed or merged any word of
    the pool or the lexicon. Mirrors load_pool in R_workflow/R/querying.R.
    """
    if ".." in str(path).replace("\\", "/").split("/"):
        raise ValueError("lexsync: pool path must not contain '..'.")
    df = read_csv_utf8(path)
    if "word" not in df.columns:
        raise ValueError(
            "lexsync: supplied pool '%s' is missing the required 'word' column." % path)
    # The same normalisation load_lexicon applies, for the same reason: `word` is the
    # canonical key behind every byte-order tie-break, so the two engines must fold and
    # trim it identically before anything is sorted or numbered by it.
    df = df[df["word"].notna()].copy()
    df["word"] = _fold_words(df["word"])
    df = df[df["word"] != ""].copy()
    df["word"], changed, collapsed = _nfc_count(df["word"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="word")
    if df.empty:
        raise ValueError(
            "lexsync: supplied pool '%s' has no usable rows: it is empty, or every row "
            "is missing 'word'." % path)
    df = (df.assign(_k=df["word"].map(lambda w: w.encode("utf-8")))
            .sort_values("_k").drop(columns="_k").reset_index(drop=True))

    reference = None if lexicon else _neighbourhood_reference(df)
    if lexicon:
        lex = load_lexicon(lexicon, schema, language=language)
        # The lexicon's own normalisation is reported with the pool's, since the run
        # read both.
        lex_record = lex.attrs.get("input_normalisation") or {}
        changed += lex_record.get("changed", 0)
        collapsed += lex_record.get("collapsed", 0)
        reference = _neighbourhood_reference(lex)
        # `id` is the lexicon's own row number, meaningless once the pool is a subset.
        dims = [c for c in lex.columns if c not in ("word", "language", "source", "id")]
        clash = sorted((c for c in dims if c in df.columns),
                       key=lambda s: s.encode("utf-8"))
        if clash:
            raise ValueError(
                "lexsync: supplied pool '%s' already has column(s) %s, which the lexicon "
                "would also supply. Rename or drop them, so it is unambiguous which "
                "values the matcher used."
                % (path, ", ".join("'%s'" % c for c in clash)))
        known = set(lex["word"])
        absent = sorted((w for w in df["word"] if w not in known),
                        key=lambda s: s.encode("utf-8"))
        if absent:
            shown = absent[:5]
            raise ValueError(
                "lexsync: %d word(s) of supplied pool '%s' are absent from lexicon "
                "'%s': %s%s." % (len(absent), path, lexicon,
                                 ", ".join("'%s'" % w for w in shown),
                                 ", ..." if len(absent) > len(shown) else ""))
        by_word = lex.set_index("word")
        rows = by_word.loc[df["word"].tolist()]
        for d in dims:
            df[d] = rows[d].to_numpy()
    # Derived after any join, so a lexicon cannot overwrite them with its own copies.
    df["length"] = df["word"].str.len()
    df["n_syllables"] = _syllable_column(df["word"])
    if language is not None:
        df["language"] = language
    df["id"] = np.arange(1, len(df) + 1)
    df = df.reset_index(drop=True)
    record = _nfc_record(changed, collapsed)
    if record:
        df.attrs["input_normalisation"] = record
    return {"pool": df, "reference": reference}

docs.text:
Left-join a norm table (e.g. concreteness, age of acquisition, valence).

norms is a data frame or the path to a CSV with a word column and one or more norm columns. This is the connector for semantic dimensions: the norm data themselves are fetched separately (licensing varies), then merged here so the matcher can equate on them.

The result is the lexicon itself with the norm columns appended, and the key is looked up positionally rather than through merge. That is what makes the two engines agree by construction, with nothing to repair afterwards, because merge and R's merge() were measured to diverge in three ways, each of them silent: R hoists the by column to position 1 while pandas keeps the left frame's order, so the column order differed whenever on was not already first; R disambiguates a colliding column name with .x/.y and pandas with _x/_y, and either way a dimension the design matches on disappears under a name nothing looks for; and R's merge(sort = FALSE) leaves the row order unspecified. A positional lookup has none of those degrees of freedom. A colliding name is now an error instead.

The key is trimmed, case-folded and normalised to NFC on both sides. Only the norm table's side was trimmed and case-folded before, so a lexicon holding Dog matched nothing and the design carried on with an all-NaN dimension. Because both engines agreed on that wrong answer, no parity test could have caught it. The lexicon's own spelling is preserved rather than folded in place: word is the byte-order tie-break behind every selection, so the join must not rewrite it.

Mirrors merge_norms in R_workflow/R/querying.R.
