    return base

docs.title: Counterbalancing
docs.text: Two recipes are available, and the paradigm chooses between them unless the design names one in counterbalance.recipe. A design's own events do not change the choice. Trial order comes from a seeded, keyed-hash shuffle, a pure function of the design with no generator behind it, so the same seed gives the same order in both engines. balance_lists is the optional search for a list assignment whose lists are equated on the item dimensions, where the plain deal goes by set rank.

docs.title: lexsync.counterbalance(stimuli, design, schema, list_of_set=None)
docs.text:
Assign stimuli to lists and a randomised, reproducible trial order.

The recipe is counterbalance.recipe when the design names one, and otherwise the recipe of the paradigm it names. That is the factorial recipe for matched word lists, or a Latin square over conditions for the paired and sentence paradigms. A design's own events list has no say in the recipe. The factorial recipe refuses more lists than item sets, since the surplus lists would be empty.

list_of_set optionally maps each set to a list, from balance_lists. The pipeline supplies it when counterbalance.optimise is on. Without it, the factorial recipe deals sets to lists by rank.

Each list's trials are ordered by the seeded keyed hash. counterbalance.max_run repairs that order so that no run of one counterbalance.run_on value (by default the condition) is longer than the limit, and refuses a limit no order can meet. A design with fillers has the limit applied by add_blocks, to the order the fillers are interleaved in. counterbalance.orders: m adds order_1 to order_m, each trial's position in each of m orders of its list, order_1 being the order trial gives.

Returns stimuli with added list and trial columns, and the order columns when there is more than one order. Mirrors counterbalance() in R_workflow/R/counterbalancing.R.

Source code in src/lexsync/counterbalancing.py 
def counterbalance(stimuli: pd.DataFrame, design: dict, schema: dict,
                   list_of_set=None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Assign stimuli to lists and a randomised, reproducible trial order.

    The recipe is ``counterbalance.recipe`` when the design names one, and otherwise
    the recipe of the paradigm it names. That is the factorial recipe for matched word
    lists, or a Latin square over conditions for the paired and sentence paradigms. A
    design's own ``events`` list has no say in the recipe. The factorial recipe
    refuses more lists than item sets, since the surplus lists would be empty.

    ``list_of_set`` optionally maps each ``set`` to a list, from ``balance_lists``.
    The pipeline supplies it when ``counterbalance.optimise`` is on. Without it, the
    factorial recipe deals sets to lists by rank.

    Each list's trials are ordered by the seeded keyed hash. ``counterbalance.max_run``
    repairs that order so that no run of one ``counterbalance.run_on`` value (by default
    the condition) is longer than the limit, and refuses a limit no order can meet. A
    design with fillers has the limit applied by ``add_blocks``, to the order the fillers
    are interleaved in. ``counterbalance.orders: m`` adds ``order_1`` to ``order_m``,
    each trial's position in each of m orders of its list, ``order_1`` being the order
    ``trial`` gives.

    Returns ``stimuli`` with added ``list`` and ``trial`` columns, and the order columns
    when there is more than one order. Mirrors counterbalance() in
    R_workflow/R/counterbalancing.R.
    """
    _trial_order_settings(design)
    # Resampled designs counterbalance each replicate (an independent item set)
    # on its own, so trial order is numbered within each replicate.
    if "replicate" in stimuli.columns and stimuli["replicate"].nunique() > 1:
        parts = [_counterbalance_one(g.reset_index(drop=True), design, schema, list_of_set)
                 for _, g in stimuli.groupby("replicate", sort=True)]
        return pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
    return _counterbalance_one(stimuli, design, schema, list_of_set)

docs.title: lexsync.balance_lists(stimuli, design, schema)
docs.text:
Assign item sets to lists so the lists match on the item dimensions.

The factorial recipe's default deal is by set rank, which balances nothing. This searches instead for an assignment whose lists have near-equal totals on each declared dimension, by steepest-descent pairwise swaps between lists. List sizes are preserved, because a swap exchanges one set for another.

The search is deterministic and identical in the R and Python engines: the objective is all-integer (see the notes in this module), the descent takes the single best swap each pass, and ties are broken by the seeded keyed hash rather than by position, so no list is favoured by being numbered first. Because the cost is a non-negative integer that strictly decreases, the search terminates; max_passes bounds it anyway and the report says whether the bound was reached.

counterbalance.scale sets each dimension's unit. mean, the default, divides by the dimension's mean, which suits ratio scales only. mad balances deviations from the mean in units of the mean absolute deviation, so adding a constant to a dimension, such as writing Zipf frequency as Zipf - 3, leaves the lists unchanged. The report then gives scale too, and cost_unit names the unit under either scale.

Five situations raise ValueError rather than being answered with an assignment that would mislead. A Latin-square design is refused because every item already appears in every list there, so there is nothing left to equate, and fewer than two lists leaves no pair of lists to exchange sets between. A design with no resolvable balance dimension is refused, as is one naming a dimension the stimuli do not carry, and the message names the columns. The last refusal is arithmetic: the search stops if the integer objective would leave the range a double represents exactly, since past that point the two engines could disagree.

Returns {"list_of_set": {set: list}, "report": {...}}.

Source code in src/lexsync/counterbalancing.py 
def balance_lists(stimuli: pd.DataFrame, design: dict, schema: dict) -> dict:
    """Assign item sets to lists so the lists match on the item dimensions.

    The factorial recipe's default deal is by set rank, which balances nothing. This
    searches instead for an assignment whose lists have near-equal totals on each
    declared dimension, by steepest-descent pairwise swaps between lists. List sizes
    are preserved, because a swap exchanges one set for another.

    The search is deterministic and identical in the R and Python engines: the
    objective is all-integer (see the notes in this module), the descent takes the
    single best swap each pass, and ties are broken by the seeded keyed hash rather
    than by position, so no list is favoured by being numbered first. Because the cost
    is a non-negative integer that strictly decreases, the search terminates;
    ``max_passes`` bounds it anyway and the report says whether the bound was reached.

    ``counterbalance.scale`` sets each dimension's unit. ``mean``, the default,
    divides by the dimension's mean, which suits ratio scales only. ``mad`` balances
    deviations from the mean in units of the mean absolute deviation, so adding a
    constant to a dimension, such as writing Zipf frequency as Zipf - 3, leaves the
    lists unchanged. The report then gives ``scale`` too, and ``cost_unit`` names the
    unit under either scale.

    Five situations raise ``ValueError`` rather than being answered with an assignment
    that would mislead. A Latin-square design is refused because every item already
    appears in every list there, so there is nothing left to equate, and fewer than two
    lists leaves no pair of lists to exchange sets between. A design with no resolvable
    balance dimension is refused, as is one naming a dimension the stimuli do not carry,
    and the message names the columns. The last refusal is arithmetic: the search stops
    if the integer objective would leave the range a double represents exactly, since
    past that point the two engines could disagree.

    Returns ``{"list_of_set": {set: list}, "report": {...}}``.
    """
    cb = design.get("counterbalance") or {}
    n_lists = int(cb.get("lists", 1))
    seed = schema.get("seed", 1)
    if _recipe(design) == "latin_square_target":
        raise ValueError(
            "lexsync: counterbalance.optimise does not apply to a Latin-square "
            "design. Every item already appears in every list there, so the lists are "
            "balanced on the items by construction; the rotation decides only which "
            "condition each item takes.")
    if n_lists < 2:
        raise ValueError("lexsync: counterbalance.optimise needs "
                         "counterbalance.lists to be 2 or more.")
    dims = _balance_dims(design)
    if not dims:
        raise ValueError(
            "lexsync: counterbalance.optimise has no dimensions to balance. Name them "
            "in counterbalance.balance_on, or give the design a match_on.")
    absent = sorted((d for d in dims if d not in stimuli.columns),
                    key=lambda s: s.encode("utf-8"))
    if absent:
        raise ValueError("lexsync: cannot balance on column(s) the stimuli do not "
                         "have: %s." % ", ".join("'%s'" % a for a in absent))

    scale = _balance_scale(design)
    sets = sorted(stimuli["set"].unique())
    n_sets = len(sets)
    V = _balance_values(stimuli, dims, scale)
    totals = {d: sum(v) for d, v in V.items()}
    # Bounded on the sum of the absolute set totals, which bounds every list's total.
    # Under mad the values are deviations whose total is near zero, so a bound on the
    # total would bound nothing. For values of one sign the two bounds are the same.
    if (max((sum(abs(v) for v in vals) for vals in V.values()), default=0) * n_sets
            > BALANCE_MAX_MAGNITUDE):
        raise ValueError(
            "lexsync: the balance objective would exceed the exact-integer range.")

    # Start from the default deal, so the search improves on the shipped behaviour
    # rather than starting somewhere unrelated to it.
    assign = [(i % n_lists) + 1 for i in range(n_sets)]
    cost0 = _balance_cost(V, assign, n_lists, n_sets)

    pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(n_sets - 1) for j in range(i + 1, n_sets)]
    max_passes = int(cb.get("max_passes", 500))
    n_swaps = 0
    cost = cost0
    hit_bound = False
    for pass_i in range(1, max(0, max_passes) + 1):
        cand = [(i, j) for i, j in pairs if assign[i] != assign[j]]
        if not cand:
            break
        n_in = [sum(1 for a in assign if a == l) for l in range(1, n_lists + 1)]
        S = {d: [sum(v for v, a in zip(V[d], assign, strict=True) if a == l)
                 for l in range(1, n_lists + 1)] for d in dims}
        best = 0
        tied = []
        for i, j in cand:
            la, lb = assign[i], assign[j]
            delta = 0
            for d in dims:
                va, vb = V[d][i], V[d][j]
                Sa, Sb = S[d][la - 1], S[d][lb - 1]
                sha = totals[d] * n_in[la - 1]
                shb = totals[d] * n_in[lb - 1]
                delta += (abs((Sa - va + vb) * n_sets - sha)
                          + abs((Sb - vb + va) * n_sets - shb)
                          - abs(Sa * n_sets - sha)
                          - abs(Sb * n_sets - shb))
            if delta < best:
                best, tied = delta, [(i, j)]
            elif delta == best and tied:
                tied.append((i, j))
        if best >= 0 or not tied:
            break
        if len(tied) > 1:
            # Hash tie-break, not position: taking the first tied pair would
            # systematically prefer low-numbered sets, and the digest is the package's
            # established way of choosing without a generator.
            def _h(pair):
                key = "|".join([_key_part(seed), "balance",
                                _key_part(sets[pair[0]]), _key_part(sets[pair[1]])])
                return hashlib.sha256(key.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
            pick = sorted(tied, key=_h)[0]
        else:
            pick = tied[0]
        i, j = pick
        assign[i], assign[j] = assign[j], assign[i]
        cost += best
        n_swaps += 1
        if pass_i == max_passes:
            hit_bound = True

    report = {
        "dimensions": list(dims), "cost_before": int(cost0),
        "cost_after": int(cost), "n_swaps": int(n_swaps),
        "max_passes_reached": hit_bound,
        "cost_unit": _BALANCE_COST_UNITS[scale],
    }
    # Recorded only off the default, so the record of a design that names no scale
    # reads as it did before the option. Its cost_unit names the mean.
    if scale != "mean":
        report["scale"] = scale
    return {"list_of_set": {s: int(a) for s, a in zip(sets, assign, strict=True)},
            "report": report}

docs.text:
Source code in src/lexsync/counterbalancing.py 
def participant_table(factors: dict, n_participants: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    keys = list(factors.keys())
    # R's expand.grid() varies the first factor fastest, itertools.product the
    # last; cross the reversed keys and unreverse each cell so a participant
    # number is allocated the same cell by either engine.
    grid = [cell[::-1] for cell in product(*[factors[k] for k in reversed(keys)])]
    rows = [dict(zip(keys, grid[i % len(grid)], strict=True)) for i in range(n_participants)]
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["participant"] = np.arange(1, n_participants + 1)
    return df

docs.title: Validation and equivalence
docs.text: A matched design claims that its controls do not differ, and a non-significant test of difference does not establish that. These functions report the realised control instead: the standardised difference with its interval, an equivalence test against a declared bound, and the variance ratio that a mean-based statistic would miss.

docs.title: lexsync.match_report(stimuli, dims, schema, roles=None)
docs.text:
Build the full match-quality report: descriptives and comparisons.

Every pair of conditions is compared on every dimension. The rows against the first condition in order of appearance, the anchor, come first, then every further pair in condition order, so a design with a single condition has nothing to compare and comparisons comes back with its columns and no rows. A dimension with no numeric value among the stimuli, such as n_syllables for Chinese or a text label, is left out of both frames.

Each row of comparisons names the earlier condition of its pair in reference and the later one in condition. The signed statistics run from the reference to the other condition: cohens_d, d_ci_low and d_ci_high are the reference mean minus the condition mean, in pooled standard deviations, so a positive d means the reference scores higher. mean_diff is the same difference in the dimension's own unit, to three places. var_ratio is the other way up, the condition variance over the reference variance.

roles (optional) is a function of (condition, reference, dimension) that returns the row's role: manipulated when the design sets the two conditions apart on the dimension, controlled when it matches them on it and uncontrolled otherwise. run_pipeline derives it from the design. Without it, role is missing. Stimuli without a condition column, or without a dimension named in dims, are refused.

def match_report(stimuli: pd.DataFrame, dims, schema: dict, roles=None) -> dict:
    """Build the full match-quality report: descriptives and comparisons.

    Every pair of conditions is compared on every dimension. The rows against the
    first condition in order of appearance, the anchor, come first, then every further
    pair in condition order, so a design with a single condition has nothing to
    compare and ``comparisons`` comes back with its columns and no rows. A dimension
    with no numeric value among the stimuli, such as ``n_syllables`` for Chinese or a
    text label, is left out of both frames.

    Each row of ``comparisons`` names the earlier condition of its pair in
    ``reference`` and the later one in ``condition``. The signed statistics run from
    the reference to the other condition: ``cohens_d``, ``d_ci_low`` and ``d_ci_high``
    are the reference mean minus the ``condition`` mean, in pooled standard
    deviations, so a positive *d* means the reference scores higher. ``mean_diff`` is
    the same difference in the dimension's own unit, to three places. ``var_ratio``
    is the other way up, the ``condition`` variance over the reference variance.

    ``roles`` (optional) is a function of ``(condition, reference, dimension)`` that
    returns the row's ``role``: ``manipulated`` when the design sets the two
    conditions apart on the dimension, ``controlled`` when it matches them on it and
    ``uncontrolled`` otherwise. ``run_pipeline`` derives it from the design. Without
    it, ``role`` is missing. Stimuli without a ``condition`` column, or without a
    dimension named in ``dims``, are refused.
    """
    _require_columns(stimuli, [], "condition")
    conds = list(dict.fromkeys(stimuli["condition"]))
    dims = _reportable(stimuli, dims)
    desc = describe_stimuli(stimuli, dims)
    bound = (schema.get("equivalence") or {}).get("bound_d", 0.5)
    alpha = (schema.get("equivalence") or {}).get("alpha", 0.05)
    rows = []
    for ref, cc in _condition_pairs(conds):
        for dim in dims:
            x = _numeric(stimuli.loc[stimuli["condition"] == ref, dim])
            y = _numeric(stimuli.loc[stimuli["condition"] == cc, dim])
            tt = tost_equiv(x, y, bound, alpha)
            ci = cohens_d_ci(x, y, alpha)
            vr = variance_ratio(y, x)
            p = tt["p"]
            # An undefined d and its interval serialise as missing cells (empty in
            # the CSV, null in the datasheet), exactly like the other missing stats.
            d = cohens_d(x, y)
            lo, hi = ci["ci_low"], ci["ci_high"]
            # The raw difference needs one value a side, where d needs two.
            xv, yv = x.dropna(), y.dropna()
            diff = _exact_mean(xv) - _exact_mean(yv) if len(xv) and len(yv) else None
            rows.append(dict(
                condition=cc, reference=ref, dimension=dim,
                cohens_d=_round_dp(d, 3) if d is not None else None,
                d_ci_low=_round_dp(lo, 3) if lo is not None and lo == lo else None,
                d_ci_high=_round_dp(hi, 3) if hi is not None and hi == hi else None,
                var_ratio=_round_dp(vr, 3) if vr is not None else None,
                tost_p=_round_dp(p, 4) if p == p else None,
                equivalent=tt["equivalent"],
                mean_diff=_round_dp(diff, 3) if diff is not None else None,
                role=roles(cc, ref, dim) if roles is not None else None,
            ))
    return dict(descriptives=desc,
                comparisons=pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=list(_COMPARISON_COLUMNS)) if rows
                else pd.DataFrame(columns=list(_COMPARISON_COLUMNS)))

Per-group descriptive statistics for several dimensions.

One row per group of by, in order of first appearance, and dimension, with n, mean, sd, min, median and max. A grouping column or a dimension the stimuli do not carry is refused. Mirrors describe_stimuli in R_workflow/R/validation.R.

def describe_stimuli(stimuli: pd.DataFrame, dims, by: str = "condition") -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Per-group descriptive statistics for several dimensions.

    One row per group of ``by``, in order of first appearance, and dimension, with
    ``n``, ``mean``, ``sd``, ``min``, ``median`` and ``max``. A grouping column or a
    dimension the stimuli do not carry is refused. Mirrors describe_stimuli in
    R_workflow/R/validation.R.
    """
    _require_columns(stimuli, dims, by)
    rows = []
    for g, d in stimuli.groupby(by, sort=False):
        for dim in dims:
            x = pd.to_numeric(d[dim], errors="coerce").dropna()
            rows.append(dict(
                group=g, dimension=dim, n=int(x.size),
                mean=_round_dp(_exact_mean(x), 3), sd=_round_dp(_exact_sd(x), 3),
                min=_round_dp(float(x.min()), 3),
                # _exact_median, not pandas' .median(): the latter reduces through
                # numpy, the one reduction here that would bypass the shared exact
                # primitives.
                median=_round_dp(_exact_median(x), 3),
                max=_round_dp(float(x.max()), 3),
            ))
    # The columns even without rows, as when match_report leaves out every dimension
    # it was given, so the frame has the header the R twin's has.
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["group", "dimension", "n", "mean", "sd", "min",
                                       "median", "max"])

docs.text:
Ratio of a condition's variance to the reference's: a distributional balance check that complements the mean-based Cohen's d and TOST.

Two conditions can share a mean yet differ in spread and still confound, which a mean-based statistic misses (Armstrong, Watson & Plaut, 2012; Austin, 2009). A ratio near 1 is balanced; a common heuristic flags ratios outside about [0.5, 2] as unequal spread. Returns None when a variance is undefined.

Source code in src/lexsync/validation.py 
def variance_ratio(cond, ref):
    """Ratio of a condition's variance to the reference's: a distributional
    balance check that complements the mean-based Cohen's d and TOST.

    Two conditions can share a mean yet differ in spread and still confound, which
    a mean-based statistic misses (Armstrong, Watson & Plaut, 2012; Austin, 2009).
    A ratio near 1 is balanced; a common heuristic flags ratios outside about
    [0.5, 2] as unequal spread. Returns ``None`` when a variance is undefined.
    """
    cond = np.asarray(cond, dtype=float); ref = np.asarray(ref, dtype=float)
    cond = cond[~np.isnan(cond)]; ref = ref[~np.isnan(ref)]
    if len(cond) < 2 or len(ref) < 2:
        return None
    v_ref = _exact_var(ref)
    if v_ref == 0:
        return 1.0 if _exact_var(cond) == 0 else None
    return float(_exact_var(cond) / v_ref)

docs.title: lexsync.cohens_d(x, y)
docs.text:
Cohen's d, the pooled-SD standardised mean difference of x and y.

None when either sample has fewer than two values, since one value has no spread and the pooled SD is then undefined, and when the pooled SD is zero but the means differ. Two samples of one shared constant give 0. Mirrors cohens_d in R_workflow/R/validation.R.

Source code in src/lexsync/validation.py 
def cohens_d(x, y):
    """Cohen's *d*, the pooled-SD standardised mean difference of ``x`` and ``y``.

    ``None`` when either sample has fewer than two values, since one value has no
    spread and the pooled SD is then undefined, and when the pooled SD is zero but
    the means differ. Two samples of one shared constant give 0. Mirrors cohens_d in
    R_workflow/R/validation.R.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float); y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    x = x[~np.isnan(x)]; y = y[~np.isnan(y)]
    nx, ny = len(x), len(y)
    if nx < 2 or ny < 2:
        # Undefined, not 0: a frequency contrast of 6.5 against 3.9 Zipf with one item
        # a side was reported as a perfect balance.
        return None
    sp = math.sqrt(((nx - 1) * _exact_var(x) + (ny - 1) * _exact_var(y)) / (nx + ny - 2))
    if sp == 0 or math.isnan(sp):
        # Two constants: an exactly-zero difference is exactly zero SDs apart, but
        # unequal constants are infinitely many. That is undefined, not perfect balance.
        if float(_exact_mean(x) - _exact_mean(y)) == 0:
            return 0.0
        return None
    return float((_exact_mean(x) - _exact_mean(y)) / sp)

docs.title: lexsync.cohens_d_ci(x, y, alpha=0.05)
docs.text:
Cohen's d with a confidence interval, complementing the TOST verdict.

The interval is the (1 - 2 * alpha) confidence interval for the standardised mean difference, so alpha = 0.05 gives the 90% interval that goes with a two one-sided tests (TOST) decision at the .05 level (Lakens, 2017). Reporting the interval, rather than only a binary "equivalent / not" verdict, makes the realised imbalance and its sampling uncertainty explicit and keeps the dependence on the number of items visible: with few items the interval is wide, whatever the point estimate. The upper limit of the interval on |d| is the largest imbalance still consistent with the stimuli. Both the interval and the TOST treat the selected items as a sample, although a test on stimuli concerns a closed population. Sassenhagen and Alday (2016) recommend describing the stimuli and entering potential confounds in the analysis as covariates.

The limits are d +/- t * SE(d), where t is the Student t quantile on nx + ny - 2 degrees of freedom and SE(d) is the large-sample standard error of d, sqrt(1/nx + 1/ny + d**2 / (2 * (nx + ny))) (Hedges & Olkin, 1985; Borenstein et al., 2009, eq. 4.20). The d**2 term carries the sampling error of the pooled standard deviation. It is negligible for a well-matched control, where d is near zero, but it dominates for a manipulated dimension and can more than double the width of that interval. TOST tests the raw mean difference, so the interval is slightly wider than the one its decision implies, and when a control's limit lies close to the bound, tost_p gives the verdict.

The estimate and both limits are None when either sample has fewer than two values, as :func:cohens_d is.

Source code in src/lexsync/validation.py 
def cohens_d_ci(x, y, alpha: float = 0.05) -> dict:
    """Cohen's *d* with a confidence interval, complementing the TOST verdict.

    The interval is the ``(1 - 2 * alpha)`` confidence interval for the
    standardised mean difference, so ``alpha = 0.05`` gives the 90% interval that
    goes with a two one-sided tests (TOST) decision at the .05 level (Lakens,
    2017). Reporting the interval, rather than only a binary "equivalent / not"
    verdict, makes the realised imbalance and its sampling uncertainty explicit and
    keeps the dependence on the number of items visible: with few items the
    interval is wide, whatever the point estimate. The upper limit of the interval
    on ``|d|`` is the largest imbalance still consistent with the stimuli. Both the
    interval and the TOST treat the selected items as a sample, although a test on
    stimuli concerns a closed population. Sassenhagen and Alday (2016) recommend
    describing the stimuli and entering potential confounds in the analysis as
    covariates.

    The limits are ``d +/- t * SE(d)``, where ``t`` is the Student *t* quantile on
    ``nx + ny - 2`` degrees of freedom and ``SE(d)`` is the large-sample standard
    error of *d*, ``sqrt(1/nx + 1/ny + d**2 / (2 * (nx + ny)))`` (Hedges & Olkin,
    1985; Borenstein et al., 2009, eq. 4.20). The ``d**2`` term carries the
    sampling error of the pooled standard deviation. It is negligible for a
    well-matched control, where *d* is near zero, but it dominates for a
    manipulated dimension and can more than double the width of that
    interval. TOST tests the raw mean difference, so the interval is slightly
    wider than the one its decision implies, and when a control's limit lies
    close to the bound, ``tost_p`` gives the verdict.

    The estimate and both limits are ``None`` when either sample has fewer than two
    values, as :func:`cohens_d` is.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float); y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    x = x[~np.isnan(x)]; y = y[~np.isnan(y)]
    nx, ny = len(x), len(y)
    if nx < 2 or ny < 2:
        return dict(d=None, ci_low=None, ci_high=None)
    sp = math.sqrt(((nx - 1) * _exact_var(x) + (ny - 1) * _exact_var(y)) / (nx + ny - 2))
    diff = float(_exact_mean(x) - _exact_mean(y))
    if sp == 0 or math.isnan(sp):
        # Equal constants carry no sampling uncertainty: a point at zero. Unequal
        # constants are infinitely many SDs apart, so the estimate and its interval
        # are undefined, not a perfect [0, 0].
        if diff == 0:
            return dict(d=0.0, ci_low=0.0, ci_high=0.0)
        return dict(d=None, ci_low=None, ci_high=None)
    d = diff / sp
    # Large-sample variance of d: 1/nx + 1/ny + d**2 / (2 * (nx + ny)) (Hedges &
    # Olkin, 1985; Borenstein et al., 2009, eq. 4.20). Without the d**2 term the
    # interval treated the pooled SD as known, which gave a manipulated dimension
    # with d = 5.6 and 40 items a side a margin of 0.37 in place of 0.83. Written
    # with d * d, not d ** 2, and summed in the same order as validation.R, so both
    # engines round every step identically.
    se = math.sqrt(1 / nx + 1 / ny + d * d / (2 * (nx + ny)))
    margin = float(stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha, nx + ny - 2) * se)
    return dict(d=float(d), ci_low=d - margin, ci_high=d + margin)

docs.text:
Write a runnable PsychoPy script and the conditions file it reads.

The conditions file, <base>_psychopy.csv, holds every presentation version (see :func:presentation_versions), and the script presents one per run: the version given by --version (or --list when there are no replicates), else the participant's by the rule ((participant - 1) mod V) + 1 from --participant, else what a start-up dialogue asks for. A version the script does not have stops the run with a message. With counterbalance.orders: m the conditions file holds each trial's position in each of m orders, and the script presents the version in order (((participant - 1) div V) mod m) + 1, or in order 1 without a participant number. The data file then records the order.

Before the first trial, the script shows the version's instructions, the design's instructions or lexsync's for its task, and waits for the space bar, which also lets the experimenter start the run. Escape there stops the run before anything is recorded. The text is embedded as JSON data, one text per version.

Each run writes data/<base>_p<participant>_v<version>_<date>-<time>.csv beside the script, without the _p part when no participant number is given, one row per trial, each written as its trial ends. A row holds the run, the trial's fields and trigger codes, the response and its reaction time from the onset of the stimulus it answers, whether the window closed without one, whether the key was the trial's answer, the self-paced reading times, the question's response and reaction time, the measured refresh rate, the trigger mode the run used, and each event's realised flips and onset.

Each trigger code goes out on its stimulus's first flip and is held for triggers.trigger_hold_ms, in whole flips at the measured refresh and never under 10 ms, through the events after it when its own is shorter, unless the next onset's code replaces it first. The session markers, 254 before the first trial and 255 after the last, are held the same way.

The script runs full screen unless presentation.fullscreen is false, when it opens a 1280 x 1024 window, and draws its stimuli presentation.text_height_px pixels high, 48 by default. It writes the codes to the parallel port at triggers.parallel_address or, with triggers.backend: serial, as single bytes to triggers.serial_port at triggers.baudrate. triggers.mode decides what happens when that device cannot be opened. Under auto, the script prints the codes instead and, before the instructions, shows a notice that the experimenter dismisses with the C key. Under hardware, it stops before its window opens, and under mock it prints the codes without trying the device. The data file's trigger_mode column records hardware or mock.

docs.title: lexsync.export_opensesame(stimuli, design, schema, outdir, base=None)
docs.text:
Write complete plain-text OpenSesame experiments and the two tables each reads.

<base>.osexp loops over <base>_opensesame.csv, which holds numbers only: lexsync_row (the trial's position in loop order, from 1), lexsync_trial, lexsync_list, lexsync_set, the trigger codes, critical_region and any per-trial duration. The presented text, condition, block and answer are in <base>_opensesame_text.csv, which the inline scripts read with Python's csv module, so OpenSesame never evaluates them. Copy both tables with the experiment.

Before the loop, an inline script, lexsync_instructions, shows the design's instructions, or lexsync's for its task, and waits for the space bar. Every trial is logged. A response after a text event is collected by that event's script from the stimulus's onset, which sets response, response_time, timed_out and correct. A response kept after the stimulus with from: offset is a keyboard_response, and a script after it sets timed_out and correct. Self-paced reading sets lexsync_region_rts and a question question_response and question_rt. A script clears these as each trial starts, another copies the trial's labels into lexsync_condition, lexsync_block and lexsync_answer, and a logger item ends the trial.

Every canvas a trial shows is built before the trial runs, in the prepare phase of its script, and each event is timed from the onset its display returns. An event ends half a frame before its duration is up, so that the next display lands on the refresh that ends it. The frame period is measured at start-up and logged as lexsync_frame_ms, with presentation.assumed_refresh_hz as the fallback when the measurement fails. Each trigger code is held for triggers.trigger_hold_ms, at least 10 ms, through the events after it when its own is shorter, unless the next onset's code replaces it first. The session markers, 254 and 255, are sent just before the first trial and just after the last, held the same way.

The setup writes the codes to the parallel port at triggers.parallel_address or, with triggers.backend: serial, as single bytes to triggers.serial_port at triggers.baudrate. When that device cannot be opened, triggers.mode: auto prints the codes instead. An inline script, lexsync_trigger_notice, then says so before any other screen and waits for the C key. hardware stops the experiment there, and mock prints the codes without trying the device. Every trial logs lexsync_trigger_mode, hardware or mock. Text is drawn presentation.text_height_px pixels high, OpenSesame's font_size, and OpenSesame takes full screen from the mode it is launched in.

A design with more than one presentation version (see :func:presentation_versions) gets one experiment per version instead, each with its own two tables holding only that version's trials: <base>_list<k>.osexp, or <base>_rep<r>_list<k>.osexp when the versions span several replicates. Each one checks OpenSesame's subject number at start-up and shows a warning when that participant would normally run another version. A design with counterbalance.orders: m gets one experiment per version and order, <base>_list<k>_order<j>.osexp (<base>_order<j>.osexp for a single version), each with tables sorted by its order, a lexsync_order variable that every trial logs, and a check that compares the participant's order too, order (((p - 1) div V) mod m) + 1. export_experiments lists every file written.

OpenSesame evaluates the cells of a loop table: in 4.x a cell holding { runs as a Python f-string, and in 3.3 a cell starting with = or holding [=...] runs as Python. A value in a numeric column that is not a plain number is therefore refused, naming the column. An empty cell passes. These rules were checked against the sources of OpenSesame 3.3.14 and 4.1.20.

def export_opensesame(stimuli, design, schema, outdir, base=None) -> str:
    """Write complete plain-text OpenSesame experiments and the two tables each reads.

    ``<base>.osexp`` loops over ``<base>_opensesame.csv``, which holds numbers only:
    ``lexsync_row`` (the trial's position in loop order, from 1), ``lexsync_trial``,
    ``lexsync_list``, ``lexsync_set``, the trigger codes, ``critical_region`` and any
    per-trial duration. The presented text, ``condition``, ``block`` and ``answer`` are
    in ``<base>_opensesame_text.csv``, which the inline scripts read with Python's
    ``csv`` module, so OpenSesame never evaluates them. Copy both tables with the
    experiment.

    Before the loop, an inline script, ``lexsync_instructions``, shows the design's
    ``instructions``, or lexsync's for its task, and waits for the space bar. Every
    trial is logged. A response after a text event is collected by that event's
    script from the stimulus's onset, which sets ``response``, ``response_time``,
    ``timed_out`` and ``correct``. A response kept after the stimulus with
    ``from: offset`` is a keyboard_response, and a script after it sets ``timed_out``
    and ``correct``. Self-paced reading sets ``lexsync_region_rts`` and a question
    ``question_response`` and ``question_rt``. A script clears these as each trial
    starts, another copies the trial's labels into ``lexsync_condition``,
    ``lexsync_block`` and ``lexsync_answer``, and a logger item ends the trial.

    Every canvas a trial shows is built before the trial runs, in the prepare phase of
    its script, and each event is timed from the onset its display returns. An event
    ends half a frame before its duration is up, so that the next display lands on
    the refresh that ends it. The frame period is measured at start-up and logged as
    ``lexsync_frame_ms``, with ``presentation.assumed_refresh_hz`` as the fallback when
    the measurement fails. Each trigger code is held for ``triggers.trigger_hold_ms``,
    at least 10 ms, through the events after it when its own is shorter, unless the
    next onset's code replaces it first. The session markers, 254 and 255, are sent
    just before the first trial and just after the last, held the same way.

    The setup writes the codes to the parallel port at ``triggers.parallel_address`` or,
    with ``triggers.backend: serial``, as single bytes to ``triggers.serial_port`` at
    ``triggers.baudrate``. When that device cannot be opened, ``triggers.mode: auto``
    prints the codes instead. An inline script, ``lexsync_trigger_notice``, then says
    so before any other screen and waits for the C key. ``hardware`` stops the
    experiment there, and ``mock`` prints the codes without trying the device. Every
    trial logs ``lexsync_trigger_mode``, ``hardware`` or ``mock``. Text is drawn
    ``presentation.text_height_px`` pixels high, OpenSesame's ``font_size``, and
    OpenSesame takes full screen from the mode it is launched in.

    A design with more than one presentation version (see
    :func:`presentation_versions`) gets one experiment per version instead, each with
    its own two tables holding only that version's trials: ``<base>_list<k>.osexp``, or
    ``<base>_rep<r>_list<k>.osexp`` when the versions span several replicates. Each one
    checks OpenSesame's subject number at start-up and shows a warning when that
    participant would normally run another version. A design with
    ``counterbalance.orders: m`` gets one experiment per version and order,
    ``<base>_list<k>_order<j>.osexp`` (``<base>_order<j>.osexp`` for a single version),
    each with tables sorted by its order, a ``lexsync_order`` variable that every trial
    logs, and a check that compares the participant's order too, order
    ``(((p - 1) div V) mod m) + 1``. ``export_experiments`` lists every file written.

    OpenSesame evaluates the cells of a loop table: in 4.x a cell holding ``{`` runs as
    a Python f-string, and in 3.3 a cell starting with ``=`` or holding ``[=...]`` runs
    as Python. A value in a numeric column that is not a plain number is therefore
    refused, naming the column. An empty cell passes. These rules were checked against
    the sources of OpenSesame 3.3.14 and 4.1.20.

    Parameters
    ----------
    stimuli : pandas.DataFrame
        Stimuli with trigger columns (see ``lexsync.scripting.assign_triggers``).
    design : dict
        A parsed design configuration.
    schema : dict
        The parsed global schema (trigger and presentation settings).
    outdir : str
        Output directory.
    base : str, optional
        File-name stem, by default ``lexsync.design.design_stem(design)``, built
        from the design's name and language.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        The path to the generated ``.osexp``, version 1's when there are several.
    """
    return _opensesame_files(stimuli, design, schema, outdir, base)[0][0]

A browser-runnable jsPsych experiment from the event list.

The same rendered events and the trial data are embedded in one HTML file, so anyone can reproduce the exact procedure online from the same materials. The jsPsych library and stylesheet are loaded from a CDN, so the machine running the file needs an internet connection; the trial data are embedded and the responses are saved locally, so no server is required either to run it or to collect them. Each of the three files carries its SHA-384 as Subresource Integrity, so a browser refuses a copy that differs from the published release. Stimuli are drawn presentation.text_height_px pixels high, 48 by default. Onset triggers are recorded in each trial's data (a browser cannot drive a parallel port); online EEG synchronisation needs WebSerial/LSL or a photodiode. A stimulus that collects its response is one trial, recorded as target: it accepts the keys from its onset, shows the stimulus for its duration and stays open for the timeout after it, a key ends it, and rt runs from the onset.

The page embeds every presentation version (see :func:presentation_versions) and runs one, named in its address: ?version=K, ?list=K when there are no replicates, or ?participant=N, whose version is ((N - 1) mod V) + 1. A page with more than one version, opened with none of these, shows a screen naming them and runs nothing. With counterbalance.orders: m the page presents the version in order (((N - 1) div V) mod m) + 1, or in order 1 without a participant number, and every data row carries the order. Its welcome screen shows the version's instructions, the design's instructions or lexsync's for its task, and waits for the space bar. The data rows carry the participant, the version, the list and the replicate, and the data file is named after the participant and the version. The page names the keys as the browser does, arrowleft for left, in its events and in each trial's answer, so a recorded response can be compared with the answer as it stands.

def export_jspsych(stimuli, design, schema, outdir, base=None) -> str:
    """A browser-runnable jsPsych experiment from the event list.

    The same rendered events and the trial data are embedded in one HTML file, so
    anyone can reproduce the exact procedure online from the same materials. The
    jsPsych library and stylesheet are loaded from a CDN, so the machine running the
    file needs an internet connection; the trial data are embedded and the responses
    are saved locally, so no server is required either to run it or to collect them.
    Each of the three files carries its SHA-384 as Subresource Integrity, so a browser
    refuses a copy that differs from the published release. Stimuli are drawn
    ``presentation.text_height_px`` pixels high, 48 by default.
    Onset triggers are recorded in each trial's data (a browser cannot drive a
    parallel port); online EEG synchronisation needs WebSerial/LSL or a photodiode.
    A stimulus that collects its response is one trial, recorded as ``target``: it
    accepts the keys from its onset, shows the stimulus for its duration and stays
    open for the timeout after it, a key ends it, and ``rt`` runs from the onset.

    The page embeds every presentation version (see :func:`presentation_versions`) and
    runs one, named in its address: ``?version=K``, ``?list=K`` when there are no
    replicates, or ``?participant=N``, whose version is ``((N - 1) mod V) + 1``. A page
    with more than one version, opened with none of these, shows a screen naming them
    and runs nothing. With ``counterbalance.orders: m`` the page presents the version in
    order ``(((N - 1) div V) mod m) + 1``, or in order 1 without a participant number,
    and every data row carries the order. Its welcome screen shows the version's instructions, the design's
    ``instructions`` or lexsync's for its task, and waits for the space bar. The data
    rows carry the participant, the version, the list and the replicate, and the data
    file is named after the participant and the version. The page names the keys as the
    browser does, ``arrowleft`` for ``left``, in its events and in each trial's
    ``answer``, so a recorded response can be compared with the answer as it stands.
    """
    base = base or design_stem(design)
    events = resolve_events(design)
    rendered = _map_keys_for_jspsych(_sized_masks(
        render_events(events, design.get("timing") or {}, _refresh_hz(schema)), stimuli))
    versions = presentation_versions(stimuli)
    trials = [{key: _fifteen_digits(value) for key, value in row.items()}
              for row in _map_answers_for_jspsych(
                  loop_table(stimuli, events)).to_dict(orient="records")]
    presentation = schema.get("presentation") or {}
    font = design.get("font") or presentation.get("font") or "Courier New"
    with open(find_template("jspsych/experiment_template.html"), encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        tmpl = handle.read()
    # DESIGN lands in <title> and a comment, LANGUAGE_TAG in a lang attribute, WORD_FONT
    # inside a CSS font-family declaration. Only the JSON blobs, the instructions among
    # them, are escaped by _json_html; the rest are validated, since a quote or an angle
    # bracket in any of them would leave its attribute or rule and start markup in a page
    # that collects participant responses.
    subs = {
        "DESIGN": clean_meta(design["name"], "the design's `name`"),
        "LANGUAGE": clean_meta(design["language"], "the design's `language`"),
        "LANGUAGE_TAG": _language_tag(design), "WORD_FONT": clean_meta(font, "the font"),
        "TEXT_HEIGHT_PX": str(_text_height_px(schema)),
        "EVENTS_JSON": _json_html(rendered), "TRIALS_JSON": _json_html(trials),
        "VERSIONS_JSON": _json_html(versions),
        "ORDERS": str(_n_orders(stimuli)),
        "INSTRUCTIONS_JSON": _json_html(_instruction_texts(design, versions)),
    }
    for k, v in subs.items():

docs.title: lexsync.scripting.assign_triggers(stimuli, conditions=None, events=None, schema=None)
docs.text:
A per-condition marker and a per-item marker, both 0-255 EEG codes.

condition_trigger numbers the conditions from 101 upwards and item_trigger numbers the item sets from 40, in code-point order of their labels, so with sets 1 to 20, set 10 is 41 and set 2 is 51. Decode an item code through the loop table, not from the set's label. The item range holds 200 codes (an 8-bit-port constraint), so past 200 sets the codes wrap and repeat, and a runtime notice says so.

events, the design's event list, says which codes the experiment sends. When it sends item codes together with condition codes, or with a code of its own from 40 to 239, the item codes skip 101 to 100 + k, the codes of the k conditions, and the design's own codes, so that no item takes a code that marks something else. Sets 65 and 66 of a 70-set design took 101 and 102, the condition codes. A design with more item sets than free codes is then refused, unless schema sets triggers.allow_code_overlap: true, which lets the item codes wrap and repeat within the free codes. Every other design, and a call without events, gets the item codes it had before. Each trigger in events is checked as :func:render_events checks it.

A notice is printed for a code of the design's own that the stream already uses for something else: 254 or 255, which the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments send when the session starts and ends, a condition code the design sends, or a code within the range of the item codes it sends.

The condition codes follow conditions when it is given: its first entry is 101, its second 102, and so on, whether or not every entry occurs in stimuli, so the same condition keeps the same code in a subset such as a practice block. A condition present in stimuli but missing from conditions takes the next free codes, in code-point order of its label. Either way the mapping depends only on the labels, never on the row order. Without conditions, the codes follow the order in which the conditions first appear in stimuli, as in lexsync 0.1.0. On a shuffled trial list that order comes from the shuffle, so a different seed can swap two conditions' codes. export_experiments passes the design's order, and the pipeline passes the order of the design's conditions, followed by any other condition in the order the item source lists it.

stim = pd.DataFrame({"condition": ["low", "high", "low", "high"], ... "set": [1, 1, 2, 2]}) assign_triggers(stim)["condition_trigger"].tolist() [101, 102, 101, 102] assign_triggers(stim, conditions=["high", "low"])["condition_trigger"].tolist() [102, 101, 102, 101]

def assign_triggers(stimuli: pd.DataFrame, conditions=None, events=None,
                    schema=None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """A per-condition marker and a per-item marker, both 0-255 EEG codes.

    ``condition_trigger`` numbers the conditions from 101 upwards and
    ``item_trigger`` numbers the item sets from 40, in code-point order of their
    labels, so with sets 1 to 20, set 10 is 41 and set 2 is 51. Decode an item code
    through the loop table, not from the set's label. The item range holds 200 codes
    (an 8-bit-port constraint), so past 200 sets the codes wrap and repeat, and a
    runtime notice says so.

    ``events``, the design's event list, says which codes the experiment sends. When
    it sends item codes together with condition codes, or with a code of its own from
    40 to 239, the item codes skip 101 to 100 + k, the codes of the k conditions, and
    the design's own codes, so that no item takes a code that marks something else.
    Sets 65 and 66 of a 70-set design took 101 and 102, the condition codes. A design
    with more item sets than free codes is then refused, unless ``schema`` sets
    ``triggers.allow_code_overlap: true``, which lets the item codes wrap and repeat
    within the free codes. Every other design, and a call without ``events``, gets the
    item codes it had before. Each trigger in ``events`` is checked as
    :func:`render_events` checks it.

    A notice is printed for a code of the design's own that the stream already uses
    for something else: 254 or 255, which the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments send
    when the session starts and ends, a condition code the design sends, or a code
    within the range of the item codes it sends.

    The condition codes follow ``conditions`` when it is given: its first entry is
    101, its second 102, and so on, whether or not every entry occurs in
    ``stimuli``, so the same condition keeps the same code in a subset such as a
    practice block. A condition present in ``stimuli`` but missing from
    ``conditions`` takes the next free codes, in code-point order of its label.
    Either way the mapping depends only on the labels, never on the row order.
    Without ``conditions``, the codes follow the order in which the conditions
    first appear in ``stimuli``, as in lexsync 0.1.0. On a shuffled trial list that
    order comes from the shuffle, so a different seed can swap two conditions'
    codes. ``export_experiments`` passes the design's order, and the pipeline
    passes the order of the design's ``conditions``, followed by any other
    condition in the order the item source lists it.

    >>> stim = pd.DataFrame({"condition": ["low", "high", "low", "high"],
    ...                      "set": [1, 1, 2, 2]})
    >>> assign_triggers(stim)["condition_trigger"].tolist()
    [101, 102, 101, 102]
    >>> assign_triggers(stim, conditions=["high", "low"])["condition_trigger"].tolist()
    [102, 101, 102, 101]
    """
    stimuli, notes = _allocate_codes(stimuli, conditions, events, schema)
    for note in notes:
        print(note)
    return stimuli

def presentation_versions(stimuli: pd.DataFrame) -> list:
    """The presentation versions a set of trials holds, in the order they are numbered.

    A version is one (replicate, list) pair of the trials, and each participant is
    presented one version. Version 1 is the first pair in (replicate, list) order,
    version 2 the next, and so on. A table without a ``replicate`` column is one
    replicate, numbered 1, and one without ``list`` is one list. Participant ``p`` runs
    version ``((p - 1) mod V) + 1`` of ``V`` unless another is chosen at launch, the
    rule ``participant_table`` allocates by. Every generated experiment carries this
    list, and ``export_opensesame`` writes one experiment per version when there is
    more than one. Mirrors .presentation_versions in scripting.R.

    Args:
        stimuli: The presented trials, with the ``list`` (and any ``replicate``)
            column that ``counterbalance`` adds.

    Returns:
        A list of ``{"version", "replicate", "list", "n_trials"}`` dictionaries, one per
        version, numbered from 1.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a ``list`` or ``replicate`` value is not a whole number.

    Examples:
        >>> stim = pd.DataFrame({"list": [2, 1, 2], "set": [1, 1, 2]})
        >>> [(v["version"], v["list"], v["n_trials"]) for v in presentation_versions(stim)]
        [(1, 1, 1), (2, 2, 2)]
    """
    keys = _version_keys(stimuli)
    return [{"version": k, "replicate": rep, "list": lst,
             "n_trials": sum(1 for key in keys if key == (rep, lst))}
            for k, (rep, lst) in enumerate(sorted(set(keys)), start=1)]

docs.title: Materials datasheet
docs.text: The datasheet is the provenance record that travels with a stimulus set: where the items came from, how they were selected, the realised control, the candidate-pool sizes, the checksums and the versions. run_pipeline builds and writes one for every run.

docs.title: lexsync.build_datasheet(design, schema, report, stimuli, source_path, artifacts, seed, engine='python', candidate_pool=None, norms=None, balance=None, blocks=None, design_path=None, schema_path=None, selection_audit=None, neighbourhood_reference=None, counterbalance_check=None, input_normalisation=None, generation_exclude=None, exclusions=None, zipf_derivation=None, trial_order=None)
docs.text:
Assemble the datasheet dictionary from the pipeline's objects.

For a corpus or generated design, materials_source["provenance"] credits the lexicon that source_path names. A lexicon lexsync ships is credited by its source, a corpus fetched into the cache by the registry's citation, and any other file by its file name and checksum (see _lexicon_provenance).

candidate_pool (optional) is a list of {"condition", "n_candidates"} recording how many items satisfied each condition's window before matching, the size of the discretionary pool the selection drew from, reported so that item-selection bias is auditable (Forster, 2000; Simmons et al., 2011).

norms (optional) is a list of norm-table provenance records from the design's norms: block. Each names a file, its sha256, the join key and the per-column coverage. Recorded because a norm table can supply the very variable a design manipulates, so a record that omitted it would describe a selection over columns of unstated origin.

balance (optional) is the balance-optimiser report from balance_lists. Recorded because it decides which items each participant sees.

design_path / schema_path (optional) are the design and schema files the run read; when given, their sha256 checksums complete the reproducibility record, because those two files decide everything the seed does not. The schema's path is recorded too, in POSIX form, since an unnamed schema is chosen from several candidates.

selection_audit (optional) is the matcher's audit record; its window_relaxations entries are recorded because a relaxed window changes what "matched" means for that condition. Its incomplete_dropped entries ({"condition", "n"}) count the candidates excluded for missing a matched dimension, which candidate_pool still includes. They are recorded because the selection drew on a smaller pool than the window holds.

neighbourhood_reference (optional) records a supplied reference the derived dimensions were recomputed against ({"source", "n_words", "sha256", "applied_to"}, where applied_to lists the recomputed columns), verbatim.

counterbalance_check (optional) is the pipeline's counterbalance_check report on the counterbalanced table. Without it, the check is run here on stimuli. The record gives the recipe that ran and the lists the table holds, or for a table without a list column the lists counterbalance() would deal. It says whether a Latin-square rotation is complete and counts the trials per list and condition. It also gives the presentation versions, one per (replicate, list) pair, and the rule that assigns each participant one of them.

input_normalisation (optional) is {"changed", "collapsed"}: how many text keys the run's inputs held that Unicode NFC normalisation rewrote, and how many duplicates the rewriting created and removed. Recorded only when given, which the pipeline does only when either count is above zero, because a merged spelling changes the candidate pool.

artifacts names the files written for the design: stimuli, descriptives, comparisons and experiments, the result of export_experiments. Each file is recorded with its sha256: the three tables, then every file in experiments["files"], the loop and text tables included, or the three experiment paths of a result that has no files.

generation_exclude (optional, generated designs) lists the known-form lists of items.generation.exclude as {"source", "sha256", "n_forms"} records. A pseudoword was refused for equalling any form in them, so they decide which pseudowords a run produces, as the lexicon does.

exclusions (optional, corpus, pool and generated designs) records the design's exclude_words as {"path", "sha256", "n_listed", "n_removed"}. It gives the file, or "inline" for a list in the design, its checksum, the number of distinct words it lists and the number of candidates it removed. Recorded as materials_source["exclusions"], because the words decide which candidates the selection could draw.

zipf_derivation (optional) is {"n_values", "near_boundary"} for a lexicon carrying freq_permillion, as normalise_lexicon writes one: how many positive rates it holds, and how many put Zipf = log10(per million) + 3 within 1e-9 of a three-place rounding boundary, where the two engines' log10 could round a derived value apart. Recorded as materials_source["zipf_derivation"].

trial_order (optional) is the trial-order record of the presented trials, which the pipeline passes. Without it, the record is taken from stimuli. It gives counterbalancing["max_run"] ({"k", "run_on", "longest"}, the longest run realised in each presentation version) when the design limits runs, and counterbalancing["orders"] ({"m", "rule"}) when it asks for more than one trial order.

design["n_per_condition"] is the request the selector applied, the selector's default when the design gives none, and items["n_per_condition_realised"] counts the items each condition holds in stimuli, per replicate for resampled sets, so a selection that fell short of the request under shortfall: allow shows it. The suggested analysis keys its by-item slope on the recipe that ran and adds a matched design's matched dimensions that vary among its items as covariates.

                    seed, engine="python", candidate_pool=None, norms=None,
                    balance=None, blocks=None, design_path=None, schema_path=None,

                    counterbalance_check=None, input_normalisation=None,
                    generation_exclude=None, exclusions=None, zipf_derivation=None,
                    trial_order=None) -> dict:

    ``selection_audit`` (optional) is the matcher's audit record; its
    ``window_relaxations`` entries are recorded because a relaxed window changes
    what "matched" means for that condition. Its ``incomplete_dropped`` entries

    the selection drew on a smaller pool than the window holds.

    ``neighbourhood_reference`` (optional) records a supplied reference the derived

    "applied_to"}``, where ``applied_to`` lists the recomputed columns), verbatim.

    ``counterbalance_check`` (optional) is the pipeline's ``counterbalance_check``
    report on the counterbalanced table. Without it, the check is run here on
    ``stimuli``. The record gives the recipe that ran and the lists the table holds,
    or for a table without a ``list`` column the lists counterbalance() would deal. It
    says whether a Latin-square rotation is complete and counts the trials per list
    and condition. It also gives the presentation versions, one per (replicate, list)
    pair, and the rule that assigns each participant one of them.

    ``input_normalisation`` (optional) is ``{"changed", "collapsed"}``: how many text
    keys the run's inputs held that Unicode NFC normalisation rewrote, and how many
    duplicates the rewriting created and removed. Recorded only when given, which the
    pipeline does only when either count is above zero, because a merged spelling
    changes the candidate pool.

    ``artifacts`` names the files written for the design: ``stimuli``,
    ``descriptives``, ``comparisons`` and ``experiments``, the result of
    ``export_experiments``. Each file is recorded with its sha256: the three tables,
    then every file in ``experiments["files"]``, the loop and text tables included,
    or the three experiment paths of a result that has no ``files``.

    ``generation_exclude`` (optional, generated designs) lists the known-form lists
    of ``items.generation.exclude`` as ``{"source", "sha256", "n_forms"}`` records.
    A pseudoword was refused for equalling any form in them, so they decide which
    pseudowords a run produces, as the lexicon does.

    ``exclusions`` (optional, corpus, pool and generated designs) records the design's
    ``exclude_words`` as ``{"path", "sha256", "n_listed", "n_removed"}``. It gives the
    file, or "inline" for a list in the design, its checksum, the number of distinct
    words it lists and the number of candidates it removed. Recorded as
    ``materials_source["exclusions"]``, because the words decide which candidates the
    selection could draw.

    ``zipf_derivation`` (optional) is ``{"n_values", "near_boundary"}`` for a lexicon
    carrying ``freq_permillion``, as ``normalise_lexicon`` writes one: how many positive
    rates it holds, and how many put Zipf = log10(per million) + 3 within 1e-9 of a
    three-place rounding boundary, where the two engines' log10 could round a derived
    value apart. Recorded as ``materials_source["zipf_derivation"]``.

    ``trial_order`` (optional) is the trial-order record of the presented trials, which
    the pipeline passes. Without it, the record is taken from ``stimuli``. It gives
    ``counterbalancing["max_run"]`` (``{"k", "run_on", "longest"}``, the longest run
    realised in each presentation version) when the design limits runs, and
    ``counterbalancing["orders"]`` (``{"m", "rule"}``) when it asks for more than one
    trial order.

    ``design["n_per_condition"]`` is the request the selector applied, the selector's
    default when the design gives none, and ``items["n_per_condition_realised"]``
    counts the items each condition holds in ``stimuli``, per replicate for resampled
    sets, so a selection that fell short of the request under ``shortfall: allow``
    shows it. The suggested analysis keys its by-item slope on the recipe that ran and
    adds a matched design's matched dimensions that vary among its items as covariates.
    """
    source = (design.get("items") or {}).get("source", "corpus")
    is_continuous = _is_continuous(design)
    controlled = _controlled(design, source)
    relational = _relational_record(design, stimuli)
    conditions = list(dict.fromkeys(stimuli["condition"]))
    covariates, left_out = (([], []) if is_continuous
                            else _covariates(design, source, stimuli))
    # The response windows the generated experiments open, and with them where a
    # reaction time starts, which the analysis has to know.
    events = resolve_events(design)
    windows = _response_windows(events, design.get("timing") or {}, _refresh_hz(schema))
    incomplete = (selection_audit or {}).get("incomplete_dropped") or []
    dropped = {d["condition"]: int(d["n"]) for d in incomplete}

    realised = []
    if report is not None:
        # A report the pipeline wrote carries each row's role. One from a direct call
        # of match_report may not, and its roles are then taken from the design.
        role_of = _comparison_roles(design, controlled)
        for _, r in report["comparisons"].iterrows():
            if is_continuous:
                realised.append({
                    "dimension": r["dimension"], "role": r["role"],
                    "pearson_r": _num(r.get("pearson_r")),
                    "predictor_span": _num(r.get("predictor_span")),
                    "sd": _num(r.get("sd")), "sd_ratio": _num(r.get("sd_ratio")),
                    "window_low": _num(r.get("window_low")),
                    "window_high": _num(r.get("window_high")),
                })
            else:
                role = r.get("role")
                if not isinstance(role, str):
                    role = role_of(r["condition"], r["reference"], r["dimension"])
                realised.append({
                    "condition": r["condition"], "reference": r["reference"],
                    "dimension": r["dimension"], "role": role,
                    "cohens_d": _num(r["cohens_d"]),
                    "ci_low": _num(r.get("d_ci_low")), "ci_high": _num(r.get("d_ci_high")),
                    "var_ratio": _num(r.get("var_ratio")),
                    "tost_p": _num(r.get("tost_p")), "equivalent": _bool(r.get("equivalent")),
                    "mean_diff": _num(r.get("mean_diff")),
                })

    if is_continuous:
        # The controls are banded by the same tolerance windows the matcher uses, so
        # the record states them here too; without them the banding is unreproducible.
        selection = {"method": "continuous even-spread (predictor spanned, controls banded)",
                     "predictor": design["continuous"]["predictor"],
                     "controls": list(design["continuous"].get("controls") or []),
                     "tolerance_k": _resolve_tolerance_k(design, schema)}
    elif source in ("corpus", "pool"):
        method = ((design.get("matching") or {}).get("method")
                  or (schema.get("matching") or {}).get("method")
                  or "standardised_euclidean")
        selection = {"method": method, "match_on": controlled}
        if method in ("joint", "optimal"):
            # The pairwise methods rank whole pairs and never consult the tolerance
            # windows; recording tolerance_k here would claim a filter that was not
            # applied. They get the cap they do apply instead, with a per-condition
            # verdict on whether it fired. The candidates excluded for a missing
            # matched value never reach the cap, so the verdict counts the rest.
            selection["candidate_cap"] = {
                "cap": int(PAIRWISE_CAP),
                "applied": {c["condition"]: bool(c["n_candidates"]
                                                 - dropped.get(c["condition"], 0)
                                                 > PAIRWISE_CAP)
                            for c in (candidate_pool or [])
                            if c.get("condition") is not None
                            and c.get("n_candidates") is not None},
            }
        else:
            selection["tolerance_k"] = _resolve_tolerance_k(design, schema)
        # Exact ties decide most picks when the matched dimensions are whole numbers, so
        # the rule that broke them is part of the selection. The salt goes with the
        # hash, which makes every tie key recomputable from the record.
        rule = _resolve_tie_break(design, schema)
        selection["tie_break"] = ({"rule": rule, "salt": TIE_SALT} if rule == "hash"
                                  else {"rule": rule})
    elif source == "generate":
        gen_method = ((design.get("items") or {}).get("generation") or {}).get(
            "method", "letter_substitution")
        selection = {"method": _GENERATION_LABELS.get(
            gen_method, f"{gen_method} (deterministic pseudowords)"),
            "generation_method": gen_method,
            "matched_on": ["length"]}
    else:
        selection = {"method": "item table (user-supplied)"}
    if candidate_pool is not None and source in ("corpus", "pool", "generate"):
        selection["candidate_pool"] = candidate_pool
    # A pair-keyed continuous design does select, over the item table.
    selection["cross_engine"] = _cross_engine(
        selection.get("method"), source, selected=is_continuous and relational is not None)
    # A relaxed window changes what "matched" means for that condition, so the
    # matcher's audit trail belongs in the record, not only in the run narration.
    # Integers only, so both engines serialise the counts identically.
    relaxations = (selection_audit or {}).get("window_relaxations") or []
    if relaxations:
        selection["window_relaxations"] = [
            {"condition": r["condition"],
             "n_within_tolerance": int(r["n_within_tolerance"]),
             "n_needed": int(r["n_needed"])} for r in relaxations]
    # The candidates excluded for missing a matched dimension, which candidate_pool
    # still counts: the selection drew on a smaller pool than the windows hold.
    if incomplete:
        selection["incomplete_dropped"] = [
            {"condition": d["condition"], "n": int(d["n"])} for d in incomplete]
    if neighbourhood_reference is not None:
        selection["neighbourhood_reference"] = neighbourhood_reference
    if generation_exclude and source == "generate":
        selection["generation_exclude"] = [
            {"source": r["source"], "sha256": r["sha256"], "n_forms": int(r["n_forms"])}
            for r in generation_exclude]

    if source in ("corpus", "generate"):
        provenance = _lexicon_provenance(source_path)
    elif source == "pool":
        provenance = "user-supplied word pool, matched by lexsync"
    else:
        provenance = "user-supplied item table"
    materials_source = {
        "type": source, "path": _posix(source_path), "sha256": sha256_file(source_path),
        "provenance": provenance,
    }
    # A supplied pool usually draws its dimensions from a corpus lexicon, and that
    # lexicon is where every matched value came from, so it is named and checksummed
    # here: `path` above records only the word list itself.
    if source == "pool":
        dim_lex = (design.get("items") or {}).get("lexicon") or design.get("lexicon")
        materials_source["dimensions_from"] = (
            dim_lex if dim_lex else "the supplied pool's own columns (no lexicon given)")
        if dim_lex:
            materials_source["dimensions_sha256"] = sha256_file(dim_lex)
    # Added only when present, so a design with no `norms:` block gets no key at all
    # rather than a "norms": null that every datasheet would then carry. Matches the R
    # engine, where assigning NULL to a list element removes it.
    if norms:
        materials_source["norms"] = norms
    # The words the design took out of the candidates, after the norms and before the
    # pool filters. Integers as integers, so both engines write the same JSON.
    if exclusions is not None and source in ("corpus", "pool", "generate"):
        materials_source["exclusions"] = {
            "path": exclusions["path"], "sha256": exclusions["sha256"],
            "n_listed": int(exclusions["n_listed"]),
            "n_removed": int(exclusions["n_removed"])}
    if input_normalisation is not None:
        materials_source["input_normalisation"] = {
            "changed": int(input_normalisation["changed"]),
            "collapsed": int(input_normalisation["collapsed"])}
    if zipf_derivation is not None:
        materials_source["zipf_derivation"] = {
            "n_values": int(zipf_derivation["n_values"]),
            "near_boundary": int(zipf_derivation["near_boundary"])}

    # A corpus design draws on every schema dimension, and so does a pair-keyed
    # design: every lexicon dimension is joined onto each member. A generate or plain
    # table design reports only the ones it controlled, so the record does not claim
    # dimensions that played no part in the selection.
    all_dims = source in ("corpus", "pool") or relational is not None
    # `or {}`, not a default argument, for the reason load_lexicon carries the same
    # guard: an empty `dimensions:` key parses to None here, which is not iterable,
    # while the R twin's schema$dimensions[keep] returns NULL and the record simply
    # carries no dimensions.
    schema_dims = schema.get("dimensions") or {}
    dims = {d: schema_dims[d] for d in schema_dims if all_dims or d in controlled}

    # The recipe comes from the resolver counterbalance() dispatches on, and the lists
    # from the table. The record used to infer the recipe from the item source and to
    # copy counterbalance.lists with a default of 1, though a Latin square without
    # that key deals one list per condition.
    recipe = _recipe(design)
    check = (counterbalance_check if counterbalance_check is not None
             else _counterbalance_check(stimuli, design, recipe))
    versions = _version_count(stimuli, int(check["lists"]))
    counterbalancing = {
        "recipe": recipe,
        "lists": int(check["lists"]),
        "complete": bool(check["complete"]),
        "issues": list(check["issues"]),
        "cells": list(check["cells"]),
        "versions": versions,
        "assignment": (f"version = ((participant - 1) mod {versions}) + 1 unless a version "
                       "is given at launch"),
    }
    # The balance report is added only when the optimiser ran, for the same reason the
    # norms record is: a key that is null on every design that does not use the feature
    # is noise in a research artefact.
    if balance:
        counterbalancing["optimise"] = balance
    # Practice and filler trials change what a participant sees but not what is
    # analysed, so the record has to state both counts: a reader comparing the stimuli
    # file against the experiment would otherwise find them a different length with no
    # explanation.
    if blocks:
        counterbalancing["blocks"] = blocks
    # The run limit and the trial orders, recorded only when the design sets them, so a
    # design without either keeps the record it had.
    if trial_order is None:
        trial_order = _trial_order_record(stimuli, design)
    if trial_order.get("max_run"):
        counterbalancing["max_run"] = trial_order["max_run"]
    if trial_order.get("orders"):
        m = int(trial_order["orders"])
        counterbalancing["orders"] = {
            "m": m, "rule": (f"order = (((participant - 1) div {versions}) mod {m}) + 1; a "
                             "run without a participant number presents order 1")}

    # The equivalence settings the report's TOST verdicts were computed against,
    # recorded so the Methods prose can state the bound it actually ran with.
    equivalence = {"bound_d": (schema.get("equivalence") or {}).get("bound_d", 0.5),
                   "alpha": (schema.get("equivalence") or {}).get("alpha", 0.05)}

    # The key the participants pressed for each condition, recorded only when a response
    # mapping applies: the design's own, or a lexical decision's default.
    presentation = {"response_windows": windows}
    mapping = _response_mapping_record(design)
    if mapping is not None:
        presentation["response_mapping"] = mapping

    reproducibility = {"seed": seed, "versions": _versions(engine)}
    # The design and schema decide everything the seed does not, so their checksums
    # complete the reproducibility record when the pipeline names them.
    if design_path is not None:
        reproducibility["design_sha256"] = sha256_file(design_path)
    if schema_path is not None:
        # The path as well as the checksum: when no schema was named, the run chose
        # one of several files, and the record has to say which.
        reproducibility["schema_path"] = _posix(schema_path)
        reproducibility["schema_sha256"] = sha256_file(schema_path)

    return {
        "lexsync_datasheet_version": DATASHEET_VERSION,
        "design": {
            "name": design["name"], "language": design["language"],
            "paradigm": design.get("paradigm", "factorial"), "source": source,
            "description": design.get("description"),
            "n_per_condition": _requested_n(design, source, is_continuous),
        },
        "materials_source": materials_source,
        "dimensions": dims,
        "selection": selection,
        "relational": relational,
        "analysis": _analysis(design, source, _response_text(windows, events), recipe=recipe,
                              n_conditions=len(conditions), covariates=covariates,
                              left_out=left_out),
        "equivalence": equivalence,
        "realised_control": realised,
        "counterbalancing": counterbalancing,
        "presentation": presentation,
        "resampling": ({"n_sets": (design.get("resample") or {}).get("n_sets"),
                        "disjoint": True} if design.get("resample") else None),
        "items": {
            "n_total": int(len(stimuli)), "n_conditions": len(conditions),
            "conditions": conditions,
            "n_per_condition_realised": _realised_counts(stimuli, conditions),
            "stimuli_file": _posix(artifacts.get("stimuli")),
            "stimuli_sha256": sha256_file(artifacts.get("stimuli")),
        },
        "reproducibility": reproducibility,
        "artifacts": [{"file": _posix(p), "sha256": sha256_file(p)}
                      for p in _artifact_paths(artifacts) if p],
    }

def write_datasheet(ds: dict, json_path: str, md_path: str) -> tuple:
    import os
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(json_path) or ".", exist_ok=True)
    with open(json_path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as handle:
        json.dump(_at_15_significant_digits(ds), handle, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False,
                  sort_keys=True)
        handle.write("\n")
    with open(md_path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as handle:
        handle.write(render_datasheet_md(ds) + "\n")
    return json_path, md_path
